summary: The frozen seam's `blockMs` JSDoc states "Blocking only engages relative to a `since`; with no `since` the default recent window returns at once." Core's own long-poll wrapper does the opposite, its test pins the opposite, the MCP tool description advertises the opposite - and two plugins have already implemented the seam's (wrong) side, so the same call has materially different backend cost per backend.
failure: `parley_fetch_recent({ topic: 't', block_ms: 60000 })` with NO `since`, on a topic with no messages. Per seam.ts:62 this must "return at once". Actual: transport/tools.ts:233 takes the blockMs>0 branch into fetchRecentBlocking, which loops for the full 60s (engine/blocking-fetch.ts:95 documents this explicitly; engine/blocking-fetch.test.ts:366-371 pins the row 'no since, topic is empty' expecting 5 fetches). Worse, the divergence is per-backend: bridge-redis/bridge-postgres block natively on that call, while bridge-nats/src/index.ts:264 gates native blocking on `args.since !== undefined` and bridge-matrix/src/index.ts:465 carries the comment "The seam engages `blockMs` only relative to a `since`" - so on Matrix/NATS the same 60s call degrades into ~240 generic re-query round-trips at block_poll_interval_ms=250 instead of one parked long-poll.
remediation: Pick one rule and make the seam say it. Core's shipped behaviour (block whenever the queried window is empty, with or without `since`) is what every other doc surface already advertises, so delete the since-gating sentence from FetchRecentArgs.blockMs and replace it with the empty-window rule; then drop the `args.since !== undefined` gate in bridge-nats and the since-gated shortcut comment in bridge-matrix so native blocking engages on since-less empty windows too. If instead the since-gated rule is wanted, fetchRecentBlocking must return the first page unblocked when `args.since === undefined`, and the tool description must be corrected.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a normative sentence in seam.ts that no test binds to behaviour'. Add a conformance case parameterized over the cross-product {since present, since absent} x {topic empty, topic non-empty} x {blockMs 0, blockMs > 0}, asserting the elapsed-time verdict from one table that the seam JSDoc is quoted against, and run it against every plugin in packages/conformance so a plugin that gates on `since` reddens rather than silently costing 240 round-trips. Pair it with a doc-binding test that extracts each MUST/ONLY sentence from seam.ts's JSDoc and requires a named test to reference it. The existing blocking-fetch.test.ts:366 block is too narrow: it grades core's wrapper only and never reads the seam text or a plugin's native path.

summary: The seam's `fetchRecent` JSDoc asserts a concrete return value for a named backend - "(the SQLite reference backend returns `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '0' }`)" - and it is false. This is the exact rot source-hygiene.test.ts was written for, but that guard only matches `bridge-<pkg>`, so a bare backend name walks through.
failure: Reproduced: `new SqlitePlugin(); await connect({db_path}); await fetchRecent({ topic: asTopic('never-posted') })` returns `{"messages":[],"nextCursor":"f573a5d4276d50fd.0"}`, not `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '0' }`. bridge-sqlite/src/index.ts:231 mints `<storeId>.<rowid>` (mintCursor, line 507); the bare-`'0'` form is a shape that backend explicitly documents as pre-dating itself (index.ts:495). A plugin author reading the seam and copying the reference value ships a cursor the sqlite backend itself would refuse as foreign.
remediation: Delete the parenthetical. It is not normative - the surrounding sentence ("an EMPTY PAGE with a REPLAYABLE nextCursor") is the whole contract, and the example adds only a claim about another package's internals that core cannot keep true. If an example is wanted, use an opaque placeholder.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'core prose making a checkable factual claim about a backend'. Widen source-hygiene.test.ts's PLUGIN_REFERENCE beyond `bridge-<pkg>`: over bridge-core comments and test names, flag a bare backend word (sqlite|redis|postgres|matrix|xmpp|nats|zulip|discord|slack|telegram) co-occurring on the same line with a code-shaped literal (backticked span, `{...}`, or a quoted string) - that is the shape a claim about internals takes, and it exempts the legitimate mechanism-family mentions the file already carries. Add a negative-control row for 'poll loop for SQLite; blocking event source for Redis' (must NOT fire) and a positive row for the seam.ts:119 text (must fire). The current rule's own fixture row 'a backend word that is not a package' declares this class out of scope, which is why it shipped.

summary: `Allowlist.has('')` returns true whenever any `post_topics` pattern matches the empty string (`.*`, `[a-z]*`, `x?`), so a caller-supplied empty topic crosses DESIGN 14's security boundary - while `parseConfig` rejects `topics: ['']` on the stated grounds that a field naming something can never be the empty string. The boundary and the loader disagree about the same value.
failure: With `post_topics: ['.*']`: `allowlistFor(cfg).has('')` === true and `.assert('')` returns a branded Topic "" (reproduced). transport/tools.ts:144 falls back to a bare `z.string()` (no `.min(1)`) whenever a pattern widens the set, so `parley_post({ topic: '', content: 'x' })` reaches `plugin.post('', ...)`. Downstream, `safeName(asTopic(''), fold)` returns '' for every shipped fold (reproduced) - an empty backend channel name (`#:server` for a Matrix alias, an empty XMPP localpart), which no plugin's charset check catches because the fold is a fixed point of the empty string. '.' and '..' likewise pass safeName unchanged.
remediation: Refuse a topic that names nothing at the boundary that owns it: in `Allowlist.has`, return false for `topic === ''` before any pattern is consulted, and give `assert` a reason naming it - mirroring the rule config.ts already enforces one layer up. Independently, make `safeName` throw (or disambiguate) when the name it would return is empty, so a fold that empties a topic cannot yield an unusable backend name.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a topic string the loader forbids but the runtime gate admits'. Parameterize over a DEGENERATE_TOPICS table ('', ' ', '\t', '.', '..', '\n', a 65-char name, the presence topic) crossed with broad patterns ['.*', '[a-z]*', 'x?', '(?:)'], asserting for each that `allowlistFor(parseConfig(...)).has(t)` agrees with what `parseConfig({topics:[t]})` would accept - deriving the verdict from the loader rather than pinning it, so the two boundaries cannot drift apart again. Add the mirrored row to topic-name.test.ts's fold table: safeName must never return '' for any fold. allowlist.test.ts's LENGTHS table starts at 1 and so structurally cannot reach this.

summary: regex-safety.ts states the ambiguity bound is PER SOURCE and that a caller matching one input against a collection "must also bound HOW MANY it holds". `Allowlist` - exported public API, and the class its own test file calls the place to "screen at BOTH ends" - enforces the per-source screen but not the count. Only `parseConfig` caps it, so every embedder that builds an Allowlist directly gets an unbounded aggregate.
failure: Reproduced: `new Allowlist(['ctx'], { postPatterns: Array.from({length: n}, () => WORST) })` where WORST is the source sitting exactly AT MAX_AMBIGUITY ('[ab]?'.repeat(16) + 'a'.repeat(16) + 'z' - the same one regex-safety.test.ts:201 derives). One `has('a'.repeat(64))` call blocks the single-threaded event loop for 34 ms at n=64, 391 ms at n=1000, and 7,553 ms at n=20000. Every source passes isRedosSafeSource, so nothing at the class boundary objects.
remediation: Move the count cap into the class that owns the screen: reject `postPatterns.length > MAX_POST_TOPICS` in the `Allowlist` constructor with an UnsafePatternError-style message, and keep `post_topics`'s `.max(MAX_POST_TOPICS)` as the earlier, better-located operator error. That makes the per-source calibration meaningful for every entry point rather than for the one that happens to run through zod.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a bound documented as per-item whose collection cap lives at a different layer'. Extend regex-safety.test.ts's 'a screened collection is bounded in aggregate' describe with an ENTRY_POINTS cross-product (mirroring regex-screen-parity.test.ts): for each of {manual `new Allowlist`, allowlistFor(parseConfig)}, assert (a) a collection AT the cap stays inside AGGREGATE_BUDGET_MS and (b) one item PAST the cap is refused. The existing block only exercises the parseConfig path, which is why the class's own gap is invisible.

summary: The `Allowlist` class doc calls the explicit `config.topics` list "the only set `subscribe`/catch-up iterate and the default scope of `parley_list_users`". The second half is stale: the default (unscoped) roster is bidirectional reachability, which explicitly includes topics reachable only through a `post_topics` pattern. A reader auditing what the allowlist's two dimensions expose is told the narrower, wrong answer.
failure: transport/tools.ts:391-395 calls `filterReachable(roster, { scope: undefined, canPostTo: (t) => deps.allow.has(t), mySubscribedTopics: deps.allow.topics() })` - the POST/FETCH dimension (`has`, pattern matches included) participates in the default scope, not just the explicit list. DESIGN 7 states it directly: the default unscoped roster is "everyone you share a channel with in either direction". So with `post_topics: ['ctx-.*']`, an unscoped `parley_list_users` returns peers on `ctx-adhoc` even though `ctx-adhoc` is not in `topics`, contradicting allowlist.ts:57.
remediation: Correct the sentence: `topics` is the set subscribe/catch-up iterate and the set a peer must reach to count as inbound-reachable; the default `parley_list_users` scope is the union of both dimensions. Keep the correction inside the two-dimension paragraph so the class doc stays the one place the boundary is described.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a docstring naming which allowlist dimension a caller-facing surface consults'. Add a table over {parley_post, parley_reply, parley_fetch_recent, parley_list_users scoped, parley_list_users unscoped, subscribe/catch-up} recording the expected dimension (EXPLICIT | POST_FETCH | BOTH) and assert each by construction: build a config with a pattern-only topic carrying a peer beat and assert exactly the surfaces marked POST_FETCH/BOTH reach it. A surface added later with no row fails as a missing entry, the way config.test.ts's CEILINGS map already does for numeric knobs.

summary: The `abortIfToreDown()` recheck after `startPushLoop` — the guard the comment says stops a presence loop being started after teardown — can be deleted and all 2273 bridge-core tests stay green. Nothing in the repo exercises shutdown() racing attach() at all (`grep -rn 'while attaching'` matches only the source).
failure: Plugin whose `subscribe` parks; `live_push.enabled: true`, `presence.enabled: true`. Call `bridge.attach(t)`, then `bridge.shutdown()` while subscribe is parked, then release. With the line present: attach rejects 'bridge shut down while attaching', plugin.posts === []. With the line deleted (suite still fully green): attach resolves 'ok' and plugin.posts === ['parley-presence'] — a heartbeat loop beating forever after teardown, advertising a disconnected bridge as online, with shutdown() already spent.
remediation: Add lifecycle tests for the shutdown-racing-attach path. Keep the code as-is.
testUpgrade: Parameterize over EVERY await point inside `attach` — `server.connect`, `startPushLoop`, and any future step — as a table of 'which step is parked when shutdown() lands', driven by a plugin/transport whose corresponding call blocks on a released gate. Each row asserts (i) attach rejects with the shut-down message, (ii) no presence beat was ever posted, and (iii) plugin.disconnect()/server.close() ran exactly once. This is a widened generator: a new await added to attach without a matching latch recheck fails a row automatically. The existing suite's nearest cases (stdio-bridge.test.ts 'shutdown() completes with a post that %s' and the failed-attach rollback table) only cover attach-fails-then-shutdown, never shutdown-during-attach.

summary: `releaseAll` is deliberately unlatched, so a `shutdown()` that lands mid-attach runs it once, and attach's own catch block then runs it a second time: `plugin.disconnect()` and `server.close()` are each called twice. The suite explicitly forbids this in the mirror-image ordering ('shutdown() after a rolled-back attach must not disconnect a second time', stdio-bridge.test.ts:265), and `seam.ts:88` never states that `disconnect()` must be idempotent — only packages/conformance/src/index.ts:493 does, where no third-party plugin author reading the seam interface would find it.
failure: Same probe as above: `attach()` parked in subscribe, `shutdown()` completes (disconnect #1, close #1), attach's abortIfToreDown throws, its catch calls releaseAll again (disconnect #2, close #2). Measured `plugin.disconnects === 2`. A plugin whose disconnect is not idempotent (e.g. one that double-closes a socket or double-rejects pending calls) turns a clean shutdown into an error or an unhandled rejection.
remediation: Either latch releaseAll for the rollback path (attach's catch can skip release when `toreDown` was already set by a shutdown that is running or ran), or state idempotency as a seam requirement in the `disconnect()` JSDoc in seam.ts so the reliance is explicit rather than borrowed from the conformance suite.
testUpgrade: Add a 'each seam teardown call runs exactly once' invariant to the mid-attach table above, counting connect/disconnect/subscribe/close calls per row rather than asserting on a single ordering; and add a conformance-mirroring assertion in seam-doc form. The class is 'two rollback owners for one resource set' — parameterize over which owner wins the race (shutdown-first, attach-failure-first, simultaneous) so a future third teardown path cannot slip in untested.

summary: `fetchRecentBlocking` never wraps its nap in `untilAborted` — the abort is only re-read at the top of the next iteration. The JSDoc at lines 19-25 states the signal is 'Observed while napping AND while a natively-blocking fetchRecent is parked inside the plugin, so an aborted long-poll returns in bounded time'. Only the second half is true. `catchup.block_poll_interval_ms` is an unbounded positive int in config.ts:162, so the nap — and therefore the cancellation latency — is operator-settable up to `block_max_ms`.
failure: fetchRecentBlocking(emptyPlugin, {topic:'ctx'}, {blockMs: 10_000, pollIntervalMs: 5_000, signal}) with signal.abort() fired at t=20ms returned at t=5004ms (measured). With `block_poll_interval_ms: 60000` and `block_max_ms: 60000`, a client-cancelled parley_fetch_recent holds the loop for the full 60 s budget — precisely the outcome the abort plumbing exists to prevent.
remediation: Race the nap against the signal (`await untilAborted(sleep(...), opts.signal)`) and re-check `opts.signal?.aborted` immediately after, or correct the JSDoc to say the abort is observed at nap boundaries and bound the latency explicitly.
testUpgrade: Make `pollIntervalMs` a DIMENSION of the existing real-timer abort table in blocking-fetch.test.ts:156 (today it is pinned at 40, which is exactly what hides this): add rows where pollIntervalMs is comparable to BUDGET_MS (e.g. 40, BUDGET_MS/2, BUDGET_MS) and keep the same `Date.now()-t0 < BOUND_MS` assertion. Also retire blocking-fetch.test.ts:505 'stops early when the abort signal fires', which manually does `await clock.advance(250)` to wake the nap — it encodes the defect as the expected behaviour and cannot fail on it. The class is 'a cancellation token checked only at loop boundaries'; the generator should sweep the boundary period against the budget rather than fixing it small.

summary: The comment claims 'the allowlist/regexes and tool descriptions are compiled a single time and reused by every per-request reactive server — no per-POST recompilation', and buildReactiveServer's JSDoc repeats it. The allowlist regexes genuinely are compiled once in `toolDepsFor`, but the tool descriptions are not: `handlePost` calls `buildReactiveServer(deps)` per POST, which calls `registerTools`, which rebuilds every description via `describeAllowed(allow)`/`topicList(allow)` and rebuilds four Zod schemas (including a `z.enum` over all topics) on every request.
failure: Read: http.ts:189 `buildReactiveServer(deps)` inside `handlePost` -> tools.ts:183 `registerTools` -> tools.ts:199/263/286/324 `describeAllowed(allow)`/`topicList(allow)` evaluated per call. An operator profiling a slow /mcp endpoint under a large `topics` + `post_topics` config is told by the comment that this work is already amortized, and looks elsewhere.
remediation: Either hoist the description/schema construction to app scope (build the tool registrations once and re-register onto each per-request McpServer), or narrow the comment to the allowlist/regexes, which is what is actually shared.
testUpgrade: Assert the claim mechanically rather than in prose: a test that spies on `Allowlist.prototype` regex compilation AND on description construction across N POSTs and pins the count (1 for anything the comment says is app-scope, N for anything it does not). Guards the class 'a comment asserts an amortization the code does not perform' for any future app-scope/per-request split in this transport.

summary: The `parley_list_users` trim of an over-limit presence page (`page.messages.slice(-PRESENCE_FETCH_LIMIT)`) can be deleted entirely and the whole bridge-core suite stays green. Its comment cites `nonconformant.ts` ('a page LONGER than the requested limit') as modelling it, but that shape is only ever driven through the paging drivers — no tool-layer test hands `parley_list_users` a page longer than PRESENCE_FETCH_LIMIT, so the only guard bounding decode work at this site is unwitnessed.
failure: Mutation `beats = page.messages` (no trim): 40/40 test files pass, 2273/2273 tests pass. A plugin returning 130k beats for the presence topic would then be JSON-parsed 130k times per parley_list_users call instead of 500 — the roster output stays bounded (computeRoster caps it), so nothing observable changes and no test notices the CPU.
remediation: Keep the trim, and add a tool-layer case that drives it; or drop it and rely on computeRoster's caps, deleting the comment's claim.
testUpgrade: Run the whole NONCONFORMANT_SHAPES table through the `parley_list_users` handler (not only through the paging drivers), asserting a bounded number of `decodePresence`/JSON.parse calls and a bounded response size per shape. The class is 'a defensive clamp at a call site that no test drives through that site' — the table-driven form means a new nonconformant shape automatically reaches every site that claims to survive it.

summary: `registerTools` and the `ToolDeps` type are part of the published API, but `toolDepsFor` — documented in tools.ts:78 as 'the single place both composition roots derive ToolDeps from config, so a new tool dependency is a one-file change instead of a lockstep edit' — is not exported. No package in the repo imports either symbol, so the exported pair serves only an external embedder, and that embedder is handed the consumer without the sanctioned constructor.
failure: A third-party plugin's composition root that calls the public `registerTools(server, deps)` must hand-assemble ToolDeps (identity, allow, presenceTopic, presenceTtlMs, blockMaxMs, blockPollIntervalMs). When a future release adds a required ToolDeps field, core's own roots are fixed by the one-file change while every external root breaks at compile time — the exact lockstep edit the factory exists to prevent, reintroduced by the export list.
remediation: Export `toolDepsFor` alongside `registerTools`/`ToolDeps`, or unexport `registerTools`/`ToolDeps` and let external roots go through `buildBridge`/`createRemoteHttpApp` only.
testUpgrade: A source-hygiene test (the repo already has source-hygiene.test.ts) asserting closure of the public surface: for every exported function, every non-primitive parameter type it requires must itself be constructible from exported symbols. Guards the class 'export the consumer, hide the constructor' across the whole index, not just this pair.

summary: A pending consent — state any anonymous caller can create — counts as "in use" for the DCR eviction guard, so registration spam can fill all 100 client slots with unevictable entries and refuse the owner's connector registration outright.
failure: Register 100 clients via DCR (open endpoint, 20/h/IP), then call GET /authorize once per client (100/15min/IP; each creates a `pending` entry with a 5-minute TTL and no owner involvement). `hasClientState` now returns true for all 100, `evictable` is undefined, and the next registerClient throws TemporarilyUnavailableError('client registration capacity reached'). Reproduced in-process: 100 register + 100 `authorize` calls, then registering `owner-claude` throws /capacity/. Because every store is process-local, Claude must re-register after every restart — so the owner's only path onto the bridge is closed until the attacker stops. The comment at line 158 claims exactly this class is prevented ("unauthenticated DCR spam cannot ... lock them out"); it is prevented only for a client that already holds an owner-approved grant.
remediation: Separate owner-approved state from unauthenticated state in the eviction predicate: `pending` alone must not make a client unevictable. Either cap pending consents per client_id at 1 (replacing the previous one), or rank eviction candidates — evict pending-only clients (oldest first) before refusing a registration, and refuse only when every slot holds a code/access/refresh record, all of which require the owner's passphrase.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing CLIENT_STATES table in oauth-provider.test.ts ('the DCR cap never evicts a client that is in use') with a second, orthogonal axis: for each row, whether the state is OWNER-APPROVED or ANONYMOUSLY REACHABLE. Then add one parameterized case per anonymous row asserting the mirror property — 'MAX_CLIENTS clients holding only %s must still leave the owner a registration slot' — driven from the same store enumeration the CLIENT_STATES-completeness test already reads out of the source, so a future store added on an unauthenticated path is classified the day it lands. The existing 'refuses a new registration rather than evicting the last in-use client' case is too narrow because it seeds only issuePair (owner-approved) state.

summary: `clock_skew_s` has no effect on `exp` at the HTTP front door: the verifier applies the tolerance via jose, then reports the raw `exp` as AuthInfo.expiresAt and the SDK's requireBearerAuth re-checks it against wall-clock with zero tolerance.
failure: Boot createOidcRemoteApp with `clock_skew_s: 120` and present a token that expired 60 s ago. `new OidcTokenVerifier({clockSkewS:120}).verifyAccessToken(token)` RESOLVES, but POST /mcp with the same token returns 401 (WWW-Authenticate error_description="Token has expired"), because bearerAuth.js does `authInfo.expiresAt < Date.now()/1000`. Reproduced over HTTP against the fake IdP. docs/keycloak-integration.md line 170 documents the knob as "exp/nbf tolerance, 0-300"; only the nbf half works, so an operator raising it to survive real clock drift still gets a bridge that 401s the connector.
remediation: Report the effective expiry: `expiresAt: payload.exp + (opts.clockSkewS ?? 30)` (only when payload.exp is a number), so the downstream zero-tolerance re-check agrees with the policy the verifier was configured with. Alternatively drop the exp half of the claim from config.ts and docs/keycloak-integration.md — but silently is not an option.
testUpgrade: Class: 'a verifier-level policy knob a downstream middleware can override'. Parameterize oidc-remote.test.ts over (knob, value, token shape, expected HTTP status) rather than asserting knobs at the verifier only — rows: exp within skew -> 200, exp beyond skew -> 401, nbf within skew -> 200, nbf beyond skew -> 401, at skew 0/30/300. The existing oidc-verifier.test.ts 'rejects an expired token beyond skew but accepts one within skew' asserts a property no HTTP caller ever observes, which is exactly what hid this; every positive verifier-level row should have an HTTP twin.

summary: The AS advertises `scopes_supported: ["mcp"]` but grants any scope string a client asks for, echoing it back in the token response and rendering it verbatim on the owner's consent page.
failure: GET /authorize?...&scope=mcp%20bogus-admin, approve, exchange the code: the token response is `"scope": "mcp bogus-admin"` while /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server advertises `scopes_supported: ["mcp"]` (reproduced over HTTP). RFC 6749 §3.3 / OAuth 2.1 require the AS to either narrow the grant or fail with `invalid_scope`; issuing an unadvertised scope violates the strictness CLAUDE.md demands at a protocol seam. Secondary effect: a hostile client controls a text field on the owner's consent page — `Scopes: administrator (approved by Anthropic)` renders as prose in the approval dialog.
remediation: In `authorize()`, validate `params.scopes` against the configured `scopesSupported` (thread it into ParleyOAuthProviderOptions) and throw the already-imported InvalidScopeError on anything unadvertised, before any pending consent is created and before the page is rendered.
testUpgrade: Class: 'a value advertised in AS metadata is not enforced when the client supplies it'. Add a table-driven HTTP case in remote.test.ts that reads `scopes_supported`, `code_challenge_methods_supported`, `grant_types_supported` and `response_types_supported` out of the live metadata document and, for each, drives a request with a value outside the advertised set, asserting the documented OAuth error code rather than a 200. Driving it off the metadata document rather than a literal means a future added scope is covered automatically.

summary: For a non-http(s) redirect_uri the consent page renders the literal string `null` as the client's identity, so the only trustworthy signal the owner has collapses and the attacker-supplied client_name is all that is left.
failure:
DCR with `redirect_uris: ["myapp://cb"]`, `client_name: "Totally Legit"`, then GET /authorize: the page renders `

A client at null wants to connect to your Parley bridge.

Client-supplied name: Totally Legit

` (reproduced over HTTP). `new URL('myapp://cb').origin === 'null'` for every non-special scheme, and nothing in DCR or /authorize constrains the scheme. This inverts the stated design of the page — remote.test.ts:198 asserts it 'must lead with the trustworthy redirect ORIGIN, demoting the attacker-controlled client_name' — precisely in the case where the owner needs it.
remediation: Refuse a redirect_uri whose origin is opaque (or whose scheme is not http/https plus an explicitly allowed native-app scheme) at `authorize()` with InvalidRequestError; if custom schemes must be supported, render the full escaped redirect URI instead of `.origin` whenever the origin is 'null', so the owner sees `myapp://cb` rather than `null`.
testUpgrade: Class: 'the consent page's identity line degrades on a redirect_uri the URL parser cannot give an origin for'. Parameterize the consent-page rendering test over a redirect_uri corpus — https, http-loopback, custom scheme (`myapp://cb`), `javascript:`, `data:`, IPv6 literal, userinfo-bearing (`https://user:pw@host/cb`), unicode/punycode host — asserting for every row that the rendered identity line contains a substring uniquely derived from the URI and never the literal 'null', or that /authorize refused the request.

summary: `hashOwnerSecret` accepts scrypt parameters that `makeOwnerVerifier` then refuses, so the provisioning step can hand the operator an owner-secret record that permanently fails to load.
failure: `hashOwnerSecret('pw', { N: 1024, r: 65, p: 1 })` returns `scrypt$N=1024,r=65,p=1$...` successfully; `makeOwnerVerifier(thatRecord)` throws `invalid owner secret hash (scrypt parameters out of range: "N=1024,r=65,p=1")`. Same for `p: 17`, and for `{N: 1048576, r: 8}` (writer allocates ~1 GB and succeeds; reader rejects it against MAX_SCRYPT_MEMORY). Reproduced. Both functions are barrel exports and examples/self-host-remote/README.md tells the operator to generate the record with hashOwnerSecret — so the failure surfaces at server boot, on a credential that can no longer be re-derived. The out-of-range row `N=1048576 at r=8` already sits in owner.test.ts's OUT_OF_RANGE_COSTS as a reader-side case; nothing checks the writer against the same domain.
remediation: Call `isUsableCost(params)` at the top of `hashOwnerSecret` and throw the same `invalid owner secret hash (scrypt parameters out of range: ...)` message, so the writer's acceptance domain is exactly the reader's.
testUpgrade: Class: 'a serializer accepts inputs its own deserializer rejects'. Add a round-trip property over the existing IN_RANGE_COSTS/OUT_OF_RANGE_COSTS tables: for every parameter set in either table, `hashOwnerSecret` must throw iff `makeOwnerVerifier` would throw on the record it produces, and when both succeed the passphrase must verify. Drive both sides from one shared corpus so a future ceiling change cannot be applied to only one of them.

summary: `subscribe()` samples its start point as `maxId(topic)` at the moment it is called, but core runs catch-up first and only calls `subscribe` later (inside `attach()`, after `server.connect(transport)`). Anything another process commits in that window is below the sampled `lastSeen`, so the live path silently never emits it — the classic 'arm the waiter after the re-query' shape, here spread across the seam because `subscribe` has no `since` parameter.
failure: Reproduced (vitest, real SqlitePlugin + core `catchUpTopic`/`SeenSet`, two connections to one file): peer posts `history-1`; core catch-up drains it and stores read-state `<store>.1`; peer posts `posted-in-the-window` (rowid 2); core then calls `plugin.subscribe(T, handler)`; peer posts `after-subscribe` (rowid 3). Observed pushed = `["after-subscribe"]`. Row 2 exists durably in the store and sits ABOVE the persisted read-state cursor, yet is never delivered to the `<channel>` handler. An idle Code session with `live_push.enabled: true` never learns of it unless the agent independently calls `parley_fetch_recent`. The same window reopens on every disconnect/connect cycle (`connect` resets `stopped`, the new `subscribe` re-samples `maxId`), so everything committed while disconnected is live-invisible too.
remediation: Surface this at the seam rather than absorbing it in the plugin: `subscribe(topic, handler, opts?: { since?: Cursor })`, with core passing the read-state cursor it just advanced to during catch-up so the live loop resumes exactly at the catch-up boundary (core's `SeenSet` already suppresses the overlap, which is what makes an inclusive resume safe). If the seam is to stay frozen, core must close the window above the seam — e.g. re-run a catch-up page for each topic immediately after `startPushLoop` returns — and DESIGN §9's 'the cursor guarantees nothing is missed regardless of cadence' must be narrowed, because it is false across the catch-up→subscribe boundary. Do not fix by starting the poll loop at rowid 0: catch-up only warms the seen-set for the last page, so that would re-emit history.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a message committed between core's last catch-up read and the plugin's subscribe arming is delivered by neither path'. Add this to `packages/conformance` (so every backend is graded, not just SQLite) as a parameterized case over an `injectBetween` hook: `catchUpTopic(...)` → `await ctx.concurrentPost(t, 1, 1)` (or a second plugin instance for backends without a fork fixture) → `plugin.subscribe(...)` → assert the windowed message is delivered live OR is still reachable from the persisted read-state on a subsequent catch-up without an explicit tool call. Parameterize over `{0, 1, 5}` messages in the window and over `{fresh topic, topic with history}`. The existing conformance case 'subscribe delivers exactly the post-subscribe tail, once, in cursor order' is too narrow — it arms `subscribe` before any writer and therefore blesses the sampled-at-arm-time start point.

summary: `subscriptionHealth()` is documented in the README as the programmatic health surface an embedder/supervisor reads, but only `state` (and `consecutiveFailures` in one case) is ever asserted on the recovery path. `health.lastError = undefined` on the success branch is graded by nothing.

summary: Retention is the one decision this backend makes on `ts` (`DELETE … WHERE ts < ?`, `SQL.prune`), and `ts` is `new Date().toISOString()` from whichever process posted. The README states the loss model purely in terms of reader downtime — 'a reader that's been offline longer than the window just gets fewer rows back on catch-up, never a wrong or duplicate one' — which reads as: offline less than the window ⇒ nothing is lost. That converse is false in the multi-writer deployment the same README documents.
failure: Two bridges share `/srv/parley.db`; bridge B's host clock is 2h behind (container/VM skew, a common case). Bridge A sets `retention_days: 1/24` (1h; accepted by `validateBackendConfig`). B posts `hand-off ready` → row written with `ts = now-2h`. A's next hourly prune (cutoff `now-1h`) deletes that row immediately. A reader that was offline for 30 seconds catches up and the message is simply absent, with no error, no diagnostic, and a `nextCursor` that advances past it. `test/retention-window.test.ts` demonstrates the mechanism directly — it plants rows at arbitrary `ts` and asserts they are deleted by age, not by cursor position.
remediation: State the real predicate in the README: retention deletes by the *poster's wall clock*, so clock skew between bridges sharing one file shifts which messages survive, and a message can be pruned before any reader's cursor reaches it. Recommend keeping `retention_days` well above the largest expected skew, or (better) prune by rowid watermark rather than `ts` — resolve the cutoff once to a rowid via the `ts` index and delete `id <= watermark`, which makes retention agree with the cursor the rest of the backend is built on.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a backend decision keyed on a timestamp the seam declares informational-only diverges from the cursor'. Parameterize `test/retention-window.test.ts`'s planting helper over a `skewMs` axis (`[-2h, 0, +2h]`) alongside the existing window x age matrix, and assert the documented invariant directly: for every retained/deleted row, deletion implies the row's rowid is below the rowid of the oldest row inside the window. Under the current `ts` predicate the `-2h` rows fail that assertion, which is exactly the claim the README makes.

summary: The top-of-id-space guard (`since === MAX_ENTRY_ID`) is a string equality test on a value whose spelling is not canonical. Any equivalent spelling of the ceiling id — e.g. a leading zero on either component — slips past it, reaches `XRANGE (<id> +`, and wedges the topic with a hard refusal instead of taking the self-heal the guard exists to reach.
failure: `fetchRecent({ topic: t, since: '018446744073709551615-18446744073709551615' })` against a live redis:7-alpine -> throws `parley-redis: ERR invalid start ID for the interval (topic lz, key 'probe:…:lz')`. Same for `'18446744073709551615-018446744073709551615'` and `'018446744073709551615-018446744073709551615'`. The canonical spelling `'18446744073709551615-18446744073709551615'` correctly heals (`ok messages=1`). Reproduced in my worktree. Because `assertMintedCursor` accepts leading zeros (`/^\d+(-\d+)?$/` + BigInt bound), such a cursor is 'well-formed', so core rethrows it and every restart hits the same wall — the permanent dead end README.md:22-26 says cannot happen.
remediation: Decide the ceiling numerically with the comparator already in the file: `compareIds(since, MAX_ENTRY_ID) >= 0 ? [] : xRange(...)`. Better still, canonicalise the cursor once in `assertMintedCursor` (normalise to `<ms>-<seq>` via BigInt) and use the canonical form for every downstream comparison and for the echoed `nextCursor`, so no later guard can be defeated by a spelling.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a boundary guard graded only on the representation the code itself mints'. In live-failure-modes.test.ts the ceiling `shapes` are all built from `BigInt.toString()`, so they can never produce a non-canonical spelling. Add a SPELLING axis crossed with the existing `states` x `shapes` grid — {canonical, leading-zero ms, leading-zero seq, both, bare-ms with leading zeros} — and grade the existing wedge invariant (`messages.length > 0 || nextCursor !== since`, plus 'no error naming a raw RESP code'). The same axis should be applied to the below-tail echo rows, so an over-eager canonicalisation cannot silently heal a live cursor either.

summary: The subscribe read loop's non-permanent branch is `await delay(100); continue;` — no counter, no backoff, no diagnostic ever. A fault classified transient that in fact never clears leaves live delivery dead forever and completely silent, which is exactly the state `reportLiveDeliveryStopped` was written to make visible.
failure: Point a bridge at a Redis Cluster node (non-cluster client) so every `XREAD` answers `MOVED 3999 …`, or at a node stuck in `LOADING`. `subscribe()` has already resolved; core keeps advertising the topic as subscribed; the loop issues ~10 doomed XREADs/second for the life of the process; nothing is ever written to stderr and no seam call ever fails. From the operator's side the topic is indistinguishable from a quiet one — the precise failure README.md:83-85 promises is prevented. subscribe-hardening.test.ts:317-323 asserts `diagnosed === false` for `MOVED 3999 127.0.0.1:6381` and `LOADING …`, so the silence is currently enshrined as the contract.
remediation: Track consecutive failures (or continuous-failure wall time) in the loop. After a threshold (say 30s of unbroken failure) write one stderr line naming the topic and the last RESP error — worded as 'degraded, still retrying' rather than STOPPED — apply capped backoff, and log once more on recovery. Keep retrying: the point is visibility, not giving up.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a two-valued permanent/transient axis that cannot express "transient but persistent"'. In subscribe-hardening.test.ts the `reasons` table has `kind: 'permanent' | 'transient'` and every transient row heals after 3 rejections, so no row can ever reach the sustained-failure state. Add a DURATION axis: for each transient reason, one row where the fake never heals, asserting (a) a diagnostic line eventually appears naming the topic and the RESP text, and (b) a second row where it heals late, asserting delivery still resumes and the recovery is logged. Generate over the same reason list so a code added to PERMANENT_SERVER_ERROR later is covered on both axes.

summary: `block_ms` has zero graded effect. It is validated by an accept matrix, a reject matrix, a null matrix and an examples matrix, but the single place its value is consumed — the `BLOCK` argument of the subscribe loop's XREAD — is asserted nowhere, so the plugin could ignore the knob outright and the suite would certify it.

Add one table driven from `CONFIG_KEYS` — 'every accepted <knob> reaches the command it configures' — mapping each knob to the wire observation it owns: `block_ms` -> the subscribe XREAD's `BLOCK`, `key_prefix` -> the key argument, `retention_days` -> the XADD `MINID` threshold, `connect_timeout_ms` -> the handshake deadline, `url` -> the endpoint dialled. summary: `block_ms` is documented in two places as `subscribe`'s shutdown re-check interval. It is not on the shutdown path at all: `disconnect()` destroys the reader socket, which breaks the parked XREAD immediately. An operator who lowers `block_ms` to make shutdown responsive changes nothing except idle XREAD churn.

All three describe a shutdown mechanism that never fires — the generation re-check after a BLOCK timeout is a backstop for a teardown that has already happened, not the thing that ends the wait.

Extend readme.test.ts's `documentedBehaviours` into a knob-driven table generated from `CONFIG_KEYS`: each knob declares the observable its prose must name, and each declares a behavioural row that pins the observable itself — here, `disconnect()` settling in well under `block_ms` with a deliberately huge `block_ms`, so the doc claim and the measurement can never drift apart again.

summary: `post` writes `in_reply_to` into every stream entry and nothing ever reads it: `rowToMessage` (line 815) maps only `sender`, `content` and `ts`, and `Message` has no reply member. The field is invisible to every consumer and to the whole suite.

Seam-level round-trips structurally cannot grade fields the Message type does not carry, which is why this hole survived.

summary: No test in the package can fail if the blocking-fetch waiter is registered AFTER the post-LISTEN re-check instead of before it — the exact arming-order invariant that closes the snapshot window. Mutating that order leaves all 646 tests green.
failure: Mutation: move `this.pendingAborts.add(finish)` / `set.add(finish)` from the promise executor into the `.then()` of the `exclusiveSince` re-check at index.ts:610. Full package suite: 646 passed, 0 failed (with a live server). I then wrote the discriminating case — LISTEN fast, the re-check query held open 300ms, and exactly ONE `notification` emitted 50ms into it with the row becoming visible at the same moment. Input: `fetchRecent({ topic, since: '0', blockMs: 3000 })`. Mutated code: returns after 3005ms (the NOTIFY found `this.waiters.get(channel)` empty, and the re-check's own snapshot legitimately predates the row). Unmutated code: returns in 54ms with the message. So the shipped code is correct and the suite is indifferent to it.

Add the missing guard so the ordering cannot regress: a case that fires exactly one NOTIFY while the post-registration re-check is still in flight, with the re-check returning empty (a snapshot taken before the row), and asserts the wait ends well inside `blockMs`.

Parameterize over: (a) when the single NOTIFY fires relative to the re-check — before it is issued, while it is in flight, after it resolves; (b) whether the re-check resolves empty, resolves non-empty, or rejects; (c) waiter alone vs. sharing the channel with a live subscription; (d) 1/2/3 concurrent waiters on the same channel. Every cell asserts the wait settles inside blockMs*0.6 AND that the message is returned. Fire the doorbell ONCE per cell — `waiters.test.ts`'s existing CELLS matrix re-rings every 20ms, which is exactly why it survives a late registration, and its SNAPSHOT_CELLS only make the row appear during the LISTEN (before the re-check), so neither is narrow-fixable into this. The same shape should be applied to any backend that arms a waiter around a re-query (redis, nats, zulip, xmpp).

summary: `post()`'s `inReplyTo` — the seam's only threading argument — is written to the `in_reply_to` column but no test asserts it, and no read path returns it, so dropping it entirely is undetectable.

Add a repo-level case (alongside packages/bridge-core/src/source-hygiene.test.ts) that enumerates `packages/*` from disk and asserts, for every package that has a `test/` directory or `*.test.ts` under `src/`, that a tsconfig exists whose `include` covers those files AND that the package.json declares the script CI actually invokes (`typecheck:test`). summary: The README's invite rule is scoped to accounts that share a listed `topic`, but every presence-enabled bridge also shares the reserved presence topic — which in per-topic (production) mode is its own invite-only room. A fleet with disjoint topics that follows the README exactly loses presence silently.

Optionally warn from `connect()` when `presence` would be posted to a room this account cannot join, or have the plugin surface a one-shot stderr line the first time a `post` to the configured presence topic 403s.

That guards the CLASS (a room every bridge writes to but no config lists) rather than the presence instance, and would also catch a future reserved/derived topic. Pair it with a fake-tier case: two `MatrixPlugin`s, `joinStatus = 403` for the second, asserting that a `post` to the presence topic rejects with the alias/MXID/fix message so the failure is at least loud at the seam.

summary: `drainForward` and `recentWindow` are the only two of the plugin's three paging loops with no `isStale(generation)` check (`backfill` has one at line 986), so a multi-page read keeps issuing `/messages` after `disconnect()`/`connect()` — against a token `disconnect()` has already cleared.
failure: Reproduced with the fake (shared_room, 40 foreign events, `limit: 5`, `p.disconnect()` armed on the first `/messages` request): the since-less read issued 8 further `/messages` requests after the teardown, and the `since` read issued 9. On a real homeserver those pages carry no `Authorization` header (`this.token = undefined` at src/index.ts:415, header set only `if (this.token !== undefined)` at line 1220), so Synapse answers 401 M_MISSING_TOKEN, which is not in `allowStatuses` — the caller's `fetchRecent` rejects with `Matrix GET /rooms/.../messages → 401: {"errcode":"M_MISSING_TOKEN"...}` instead of standing down and returning the page it had. The package's own `reconnect-lifecycle.fake.test.ts` asserts the opposite invariant (`POST_TEARDOWN_FORBIDDEN` includes `/messages$`), but its fixture room holds a single page, so the loop exits on `chunk.length === 0` before a second page can be issued and the guard can never fire.
remediation: Add the same `!this.isStale(generation)` condition `backfill` already uses to both paging loops (capture `generation` on entry, thread it from `fetchRecent`/`fetchSince`), and return what has been collected so far rather than continuing — for `recentWindow` that is the partial window plus its tail token, for `drainForward` the messages already collected plus `cursorPastForeignBlock`.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing teardown table over PAGE DEPTH as well as phase: seed each row's room with `pages × limit` events of noise so every paging call site provably issues more than one page, and assert zero `/messages` after the teardown. Generalize the row set from named drivers to "every seam call that can page" so a fourth paging loop added later is graded the day it appears; a `pages ∈ {1, 2, 5}` axis would have caught this while `pages = 1` cannot.

summary: Every fake-tier test grades the `@parley-stream:` cursor's REPLAYABILITY but never its POSITION, so a mutation that mints it at the room's start instead of the timeline tip leaves all 396 fake tests green; only the live conformance suite (skipped whenever no homeserver answers) catches it.
failure: Mutation `tailToken ??= start` → `tailToken = start ?? tailToken` in `recentWindow` (src/index.ts:825) makes an empty/all-foreign window mint the token of the LAST backward page it walked — the room's beginning — instead of the tip. `PARLEY_MATRIX_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9 npx vitest run packages/bridge-matrix` → 396 passed, 0 failed. Only `seam conformance: matrix > fetchRecent on a never-posted topic returns an empty page with a replayable cursor` fails, and only when Synapse is up. Shipped, that regression makes a read-state cursor for an empty topic point at the room's origin, so the next catch-up re-reads the whole room for that topic (in `shared_room` mode, every topic's traffic) and re-emits history the session had already seen.
remediation: Nothing to fix in src (current code is correct); close the grading hole — the class is "a cursor whose position, as opposed to its replayability, nothing asserts".
testUpgrade: Add a row to the fake-tier `CURSOR_ORIGINS` table asserting cursor STABILITY, not just drainability: mint the cursor on a room that already holds `pages × limit` foreign events, immediately replay it, and assert `messages == []` AND `nextCursor === the minted cursor` (the conformance suite's assertion, moved down a tier). Parameterize over how many backward pages the window had to walk (1, 2, 5) — that axis is exactly what makes a first-page and a last-page token differ, and one page cannot tell them apart. Apply the same shape to the `@parley-stream:`-with-no-token form minted when the room does not exist yet.

summary: DESIGN §6's Matrix row states the cursor is the `event_id` and that a pagination token "is not the cursor", but the plugin emits a second, structurally different cursor form (`@parley-stream:<pagination token>`) that a read-state file will actually hold for any empty or all-foreign window.
failure: Read DESIGN.md §6 Matrix row, then run the shipped bin: `parley_fetch_recent` on a fresh topic returns `{"messages": [], "nextCursor": "@parley-stream:t7-346_0_0_0_0_0_0_0_0_0_0_0_0"}` (observed against a live Synapse via `packages/bridge-matrix/dist/cli.js`). A reader of DESIGN who inspects a `read-state.json` — or who writes core-side tooling assuming Matrix cursors are `$event_id`s — meets a form the source of truth does not list, even though the same section documents the analogous composite form for Telegram and Slack.
remediation: Extend DESIGN §6's Matrix bullet with the second form and when it is minted (a window that held no belonging message), mirroring the wording the package README already carries, and reword "it is not the cursor" to name the `/sync` token specifically so it does not read as excluding `/messages` pagination tokens.
testUpgrade: Generalize the README's cursor-shape check into a doc-parity test the whole repo can run: `SHAPES` in `recent-window-and-cursor.fake.test.ts` already enumerates every form the plugin emits, so assert that each shape's literal marker (`@parley-stream:`) appears in BOTH `packages/bridge-matrix/README.md` and DESIGN.md's §6 backend row. That guards the class — a cursor form added later that only one document knows about — rather than this instance.

summary: `roomLocalpart` applies `safeName` for charset legality but nothing bounds the resulting alias to Matrix's 255-byte limit, so a long topic fails with a raw homeserver error that names neither the topic nor the plugin, while the read path for the same topic reads as "empty" forever.
failure: Against a live Synapse: `post(asTopic('x'.repeat(300)), …)` rejects with `createRoom failed (400) and alias unresolved: {"errcode":"M_INVALID_PARAM","error":"Can't create aliases longer than 255 characters"}` — no `[parley-matrix]` prefix, no topic name, no statement that the topic is the cause. `fetchRecent` on the same topic returns `{"messages":[],"nextCursor":"@parley-stream:"}`, indistinguishable from a topic nobody has posted to yet, so an agent sees a topic that silently never works. Core caps `post_topics` count but not topic length, and `safeName`'s own error text anticipates exactly this ("the disambiguating suffix does not survive the backend name rules (a length limit…)") without any backend passing it a length bound.
remediation: Bound the alias in `roomLocalpart`: truncate the sanitized part so `#<localpart>:<server_name>` fits 255 bytes and keep `safeName`'s hash suffix intact (or add a `maxLen` option to `safeName` so the fold stays injective in one place), and fail fast with a `[parley-matrix]`-prefixed error naming the topic and the limit if truncation cannot preserve injectivity.
testUpgrade: Extend the `FOLDS` table in `room-isolation.fake.test.ts` — which already asserts `Buffer.byteLength(alias) <= 255` for its short rows and so states the invariant without exercising it — with generated length rows at the boundary (`server_name` length + localpart of 200/254/255/256/1024 bytes, plus a multi-byte-UTF-8 row where character count and byte count diverge), asserting each still yields a legal, injective alias or a plugin-prefixed error naming the topic. That guards the class for any backend name rule with a length cap.

summary: `post` contains a no-op `void identity;` guarded by a comment that justifies a design choice rather than warning off a risky action — the repo has no linter requiring the reference, so the statement is dead code and the comment is the kind CLAUDE.md routes to the commit message and the README.
failure: `packages/bridge-matrix/src/index.ts:457-458`: `// identity is the logical sender; on Matrix the homeserver stamps 'sender' as our user_id.` followed by `void identity;`. There is no ESLint/Biome config in the repo and `tsconfig.base.json` sets neither `noUnusedLocals` nor `noUnusedParameters`, so nothing requires the reference; deleting both lines compiles and leaves the suite green. The same fact is already stated three times in the README (seam table, the blockquote, and "Multiple concurrent sessions"), so this is a fourth copy that can rot against them.
remediation: Delete `void identity;` and its comment. The parameter stays in the signature because the seam defines it; the README already carries the behaviour, and the reasoning belongs in the commit message.
testUpgrade: Extend `comment-hygiene.test.ts` — which already scans for tracker tags and cross-block restatements — with a rule for the class: flag statement-expressions whose only effect is to reference a parameter (`/^\s*void\s+[A-Za-z_$][\w$]*;\s*$/`), and flag comment blocks that restate a claim also present in the package README (reuse the existing `words`/span machinery across `src/**` and `README.md`). Both are properties of the file set, so they hold for whatever the next such comment attaches to.

summary: post() registers its pendingPosts correlator and a 15 s reflection timer BEFORE `await this.require().send(message)`; when send rejects the entry and timer are never cleaned up and the correlator's promise is orphaned, so its eventual rejection is unhandled — which is a process kill under Node's default unhandled-rejections=throw.
failure: Room already joined (cached resolved join), then the stream drops so `client.send()` rejects — the ordinary shape of a reconnect. `post(t1, 'a', 'hi')` rejects with 'stream closed' as it should, but `pendingPosts.size === 1` and one timer stays armed. 15 s later the orphan rejects with 'post reflection timeout in t1@muc.parley.local'; a `disconnect()` in the meantime rejects it immediately with 'disconnecting', and a reconnect with 'reconnected; retry post'. Reproduced: after the failed post, `plugin.disconnect()` fires `unhandledRejection` with `Error: disconnecting`, with nothing anywhere holding that promise. In the shipped `parley-xmpp` MCP server that terminates the bridge.
remediation: Send first and register second, or wrap the send: `try { await this.require().send(message) } catch (err) { const pp = this.pendingPosts.get(originId); this.pendingPosts.delete(originId); pp?.reject(err instanceof Error ? err : new Error(String(err))); throw err }` — settling the registered entry through its own reject path clears the timer and returns the one promise the caller is holding, so nothing is ever left un-awaited. The same audit applies to `configureRoom(room).finally(() => pending.resolve())` (line 834), whose rejected result is likewise discarded.
testUpgrade: Widen the existing `XMPP seam calls on a plugin that is not serving arm nothing` table (test/pending-registry.test.ts) — today it only reaches states where the failure happens *before* registration, so it cannot see this class. Add a third axis 'the transport fails at each stage of the call': send() rejects, iqCaller.request() rejects, and the stream dies mid-await, crossed with every seam entry point (post / fetchRecent / fetchRecent+blockMs / subscribe). Each cell must (a) settle the caller, (b) satisfy `expectNoLeaks`, (c) leave `vi.getTimerCount() === 0`, and (d) register a `process.on('unhandledRejection')` collector that must stay empty after the plugin is disconnected and the timers advanced past POST_TIMEOUT_MS. The unhandled-rejection collector is the part that generalises: it catches any future 'promise created before a failable await' anywhere in the plugin, not just this line.

summary: connect() assigns `this.xmpp` only AFTER `await xmpp.start()`, so a connect that fails leaves the constructed @xmpp/client — whose `@xmpp/reconnect` plugin is already listening for 'disconnect' — retrying forever, and `disconnect()` cannot stop it because `this.xmpp` is undefined.
failure: `plugin.connect({ service: 'xmpp://127.0.0.1:<dead-port>', password: 'a-real-secret' })` rejects, as the caller expects. Reproduced against an in-process TCP listener that counts connections and destroys each socket: 2 connections by the time connect() rejects, 6 after a further 3.5 s, 8 after `await plugin.disconnect()` and 2.5 s more — a ~1 Hz reconnect loop that outlives both connect() and disconnect(), plus an unhandled `ECONNREFUSED` rejection from inside the loop. With a wrong password the same loop re-presents `backend_config.password` to the server once a second indefinitely from a plugin whose caller believes the connection failed cleanly (fail2ban / account-lockout territory), and it holds the event loop open so a supervisor that retries connect() accumulates one loop per attempt.
remediation: Set `this.xmpp = xmpp` before `await xmpp.start()`, or `try { await xmpp.start() } catch (err) { await xmpp.stop().catch(() => undefined); throw err }`. Note test/live-xmpp.ts's `canAuth` already does exactly this teardown in its own catch — the plugin should not be less careful than its own fixture.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'a seam lifecycle call that FAILS leaves no live transport behind' case that owns a throwaway `net` listener and counts connections, crossed over the ways connect can fail (connection refused, socket accepted then destroyed, stream opened then SASL refused, start() timing out). Each row: connect() rejects, then after >3x the library's 1 s reconnect delay the connection count must be unchanged, and `unhandledRejection` must not have fired. Existing coverage cannot catch this class because every connect-path test mocks `@xmpp/client` with a FakeXmpp that has no reconnect behaviour at all — so the fake needs a `reconnectsOnDisconnect` mode, or the case has to use the real client.

summary: bridge-xmpp ships no `tsconfig.test.json` and no `typecheck`/`typecheck:test` script, so CI's `npm run typecheck:test --workspaces --if-present` silently skips it and its ~4,700-line test surface — which reaches ~15 private members through `as unknown as XmppPrivate` casts — is compiled by nothing.
failure: `npm run typecheck:test -w @sharptrick/parley-xmpp --if-present` exits 0 having done nothing (contrast bridge-matrix, bridge-sqlite, bridge-slack, bridge-net-util, conformance, which all run). I wrote the missing `tsconfig.test.json` (a copy of bridge-matrix's) and type-checked the suite for the first time: 12 real errors, e.g. `test/mam-provenance.test.ts(88,30): TS18047: 'i.body' is possibly 'null'`, `test/long-poll-query-budget.test.ts(95,5): TS2322: Type '() => number' is not assignable to type '(room: string) => void | Promise<void>'`, and 7 × `XmppBackendConfig is not assignable to BackendConfig` where the live suites call `plugin.connect(BASE)`. The consequence is silent coverage loss, not just untidiness: `XmppPrivate` is a hand-written cast, so renaming a private field (e.g. `mamPage`) leaves `priv(plugin).mamPage = 1` in test/archive-admission.test.ts writing a dead property — the 'page of nothing-but-unadmitted items' case then runs at the default page size of 200, no longer exercises the paging loop it exists for, and still passes. ci.yml's own comment claims this step means 'no fixture in the repo is ever seen by a compiler' is fixed; for this package it is not.
remediation: Add `packages/bridge-xmpp/tsconfig.test.json` (`include: ['src/**/*','test/**/*']`, `noEmit`, path-mapping `@sharptrick/parley-xmpp` to `./src/index.ts`) and a `"typecheck:test": "tsc -p tsconfig.test.json"` script, then fix the 12 diagnostics. Better still, replace `--if-present` with a check that every package HAS the script, so absence is a red build rather than a skip.
testUpgrade: Ratchet the class rather than this package: port bridge-sqlite's `typecheck-coverage.test.ts` idea into a repo-wide case that enumerates `packages/*`, and for each asserts (a) a `tsconfig.test.json` exists, (b) `package.json` declares a `typecheck:test` script pointing at it, and (c) `tsc --showConfig -p` on it names every `.ts` file under the package — so a new package, or a test directory added to an existing one, cannot fall outside every project. That is the only shape that survives `--if-present`, which by construction turns a missing script into a pass.

summary: `assertMamAvailable` memoizes with `this.mamCheck ??= this.discoMam(room)`; a rejected promise is not `undefined`, so once the first probe fails the rejection is cached for the whole connection — while `ensureJoinedRoom` still drops the join cache and re-drives the join, meaning every retry sends the presence that auto-creates a persistent room and only then fails on the stale rejection.
failure: Server without `muc_mam`. `subscribe('ops')` → doJoin succeeds (the MUC creates room `ops@muc.parley.local`, the plugin submits the persistent-room config) → discoMam throws, mamCheck now holds that rejection. Operator enables muc_mam and reloads Prosody. Every later `post`/`subscribe` on any topic still rejects with the same '<first room> does not advertise urn:xmpp:mam:2' message — naming a room that is not the one being addressed — until the bridge process is restarted, and each attempt has meanwhile created and made persistent another room that nothing ever reclaims. Mutation-tested: replacing the memoization with a fresh per-room probe leaves all 1133 tests green, so no test covers this at all.
remediation: Cache only success: `this.mamCheck = this.discoMam(room).catch((err) => { this.mamCheck = undefined; throw err })`, or drop the memo entirely (the probe is one disco round trip per join and the mutation shows nothing depends on it being once-per-connection). Either way move `assertMamAvailable` ahead of the join presence so a MAM-less server cannot mint a persistent room per retry, and phrase the error against the room actually being joined.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized 'a prerequisite that fails and is then fixed recovers without a reconnect' case: for each fault in test/mam-prerequisite.test.ts's table, drive the failing seam call, clear the fault on the FakeXmpp, and assert the next call succeeds — plus assert `fake.rooms.size` did not grow across the failing attempts. This generalises past MAM to every `??=`-memoized probe in the plugin (`nickAdoption` is the other one), which is the recurring shape.

summary: `resolveIdentity` returns `nickFor(handle)` unconditionally, but the README states `backendRef` is 'the MUC nick the handle occupies rooms under … so it matches the senderHandle that handle reads back as' — which is false whenever `backend_config.nick` is pinned, after a `conflict` reverts to the provisional nick, or for any handle after the first (the 'One bridge is one sender' collapse the same README documents).
failure: `connect({ nick: 'session-a' })`, then `post(t, asHandle('bob'), 'hi')` archives the message under sender `session-a`. `resolveIdentity(asHandle('bob'))` returns `{ backendRef: 'bob' }` — a name no message in any room will ever carry. Same for the collapse case: after a first post as `alice`, `resolveIdentity('carol')` answers `carol` while carol's messages read back as `alice`. Pinning `nick` is a configuration the README explicitly recommends ('Pin nick to a free name to fix this permanently'), so the contradiction is between two paragraphs of one document.
remediation: Return the nick this connection will actually post under — `{ handle, backendRef: this.adoptedNick ?? (pinned nick) ?? nickFor(handle) }` — or, if the fold is deliberately the answer, correct the README row to say `backendRef` is the fold this handle WOULD take as its own bridge's nick and is not the sender when `nick` is pinned or the connection has already adopted another handle. Nothing in core consumes `resolveIdentity` today, which is why this has been invisible; that also makes it cheap to fix now rather than when something starts trusting it.
testUpgrade: Add a table crossing nick provenance (unset / pinned / reverted after conflict / adopted from an earlier post's handle) with the handle being resolved (the adopted one / a different one), asserting `resolveIdentity(h).backendRef` equals the `senderHandle` that `post(topic, h, …)` actually reads back as through `fetchRecent`. Grading backendRef against an observed senderHandle rather than against a string literal is what makes the case survive a future change to the fold, and it is the same shape that would catch the equivalent drift in any backend declaring `carriesSenderIdentity: false`.

summary: `roomJid` and `nickFor` refuse an over-long JID localpart/resource up front with an error naming the plugin and the limit, but `validateBackendConfig` applies no length check at all, so the same 1023-byte ceiling is enforced for caller-supplied topics and handles and silently skipped for `nick`, `username`, `domain` and `muc_service`.
failure: `backend_config: { nick: 'x'.repeat(2000) }` passes validation, the client connects, and the first join sends `<presence to='room@muc.parley.local/xxx…'>` which the server bounces `jid-malformed` — a condition not in RETRYABLE_CONDITIONS and not in NOT_AN_OCCUPANT_CONDITIONS, so the operator gets a bare 'MUC join error (jid-malformed)' naming neither `parley-xmpp` nor the key, which is precisely the diagnostic failure the unknown-key check at line 209 exists to prevent. `muc_service` of the same length is worse: every room JID on the connection is malformed, and `roomJid`'s length guard measures only `local`, so it never fires.
remediation: Add a byte-length check to `validateBackendConfig` for `JID_PART_KEYS` plus `nick`, reusing `JID_PART_MAX_BYTES` and the existing `bad(key, reason)` phrasing, measured with `Buffer.byteLength` (the folded paths are ASCII so `.length` is safe there, but config values are not).
testUpgrade: Extend the existing `backend-config.test.ts` `wrongValues` generator with a per-key boundary axis — length 1023 (accepted) and 1024 (refused by name) for every key that becomes part of a JID — driven off `JID_PART_KEYS`/`CONFIG_KEYS` rather than hand-listed, so a key added to the config surface brings its own boundary rows. That is the same generator shape that already makes the unknown-key and wrong-type rows total.

summary: `fetchRecent` is a read that WRITES: it goes through `withStream` -> `ensureStream`, so every caller-named topic provisions a durable JetStream stream. Combined with `post_topics` regex reach (DESIGN §14 explicitly the ad-hoc-topic surface, and CLAUDE.md's "inbound is untrusted"), a prompt-injected agent can spend the operator's cluster storage/stream budget with pure reads that write nothing. bridge-matrix hardened exactly this class — `existingRoom()` exists precisely so read paths do not spend the homeserver's room-creation budget on an untrusted topic name — and bridge-nats never got the same treatment.
failure: config `post_topics: ["ctx-.*"]`, backend nats. Loop `parley_fetch_recent({topic: "ctx-<n>"})` for n=1..N: each call returns an empty page AND leaves a permanent stream behind. Reproduced live against nats:2.10-alpine: five `fetchRecent` calls on never-posted topics produced streams PROBE_never-posted-0..4 with no post ever issued. Nothing prunes them (`retention_days` is unset by default, and an empty stream's max_age never fires).
remediation: Split the read path off `ensureStream`, mirroring `bridge-matrix`'s `existingRoom`: `fetchRecent` should `streams.info` and, on 404, return an empty page (or `NoSuchTopicError`, the arm the conformance suite already permits) instead of creating the stream. Keep provisioning on `post` and on `subscribe` (both are gated by the explicit `topics` allowlist / a real write). If the long-poll branch needs a stream to exist, have it poll for one rather than create it.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a case over EVERY seam method x {topic already provisioned, topic never provisioned} asserting which methods may leave a server-side object behind — a table row per (method, pre-state) with the expected stream count after the call, so a future method or a future `withStream` call site is undefended-by-default. resource-live.test.ts's `creators` table already enumerates the consumer-creating paths; widen it to STREAM creation and add the never-posted-topic pre-state, which no current row has. Add a live row that calls `fetchRecent` on 20 distinct fresh topics and asserts `jsm.streams.list()` grew by 0.

summary: `disconnect()` landing while `subscribe`'s background loop is between `consumers.add` and its first delivery orphans a server-side ephemeral consumer. Two independent holes: (a) the closer registered at subscribe time reads `currentName`, which is only assigned after `consumers.add` RESOLVES, so a teardown in that window deletes nothing; (b) the loop's own fallback `deleteConsumer` (lines 545, 599) reads `this.jsm` LATE, and `disconnect()` clears `this.jsm` as soon as its closers return — the exact hazard `pull()` documents at line 375 and defends against by capturing `jsm` at entry. `subscribe` never got that treatment. The orphan survives for `INACTIVE_NS` (30 s) and they accumulate, which is precisely the per-Code-session restart pattern DESIGN §10 describes.
failure: Against a live nats:2.10-alpine: sweep `pause` from 0..25 ms over {connect; subscribe(topic); sleep(pause); disconnect()}; then `jsm.consumers.list(stream)`. Offsets 0 ms and 2 ms each left one consumer behind and the count stayed at 2 for the rest of the sweep — i.e. orphans that no later cycle reclaims. Expected 0 consumers after every `disconnect()`; got a monotonically accumulating orphan set bounded only by the 30 s server GC.
remediation: Capture `const jsm = this.requireJsm()` once at the top of `subscribe` and use it in `deleteConsumer` (as `pull`/`blockingFetch` already do), and make the registered closer able to reap a consumer created after it ran — e.g. have the loop publish `currentName` through a slot the closer re-reads after awaiting the in-flight `consumers.add`, or have the closer set a `torn-down` flag the loop checks immediately after `consumers.add` and deletes on.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'teardown at an arbitrary point of a resource's bring-up leaves nothing behind' with a live, parameterized offset sweep: for offset in [0,1,2,3,5,10,25,100,400] ms, connect/subscribe/sleep(offset)/disconnect, then assert `consumerCount(stream) === 0` AND that the count does not grow across repeated cycles. The two existing guards cannot fail here: resource-live.test.ts's cycle test calls `waitForAsync(consumerCount >= 1)` BEFORE disconnecting — deliberately stepping past the window — and recovery.test.ts's pauseMs sweep [0,400,800,1200] is fake-backed, where `deleteConsumer` cannot observe a cleared `this.jsm`. Widen the same sweep over `fetchRecent`/`blockMs` in flight too.

summary: `connect()` overwrites `this.nc` without closing the connection already held. The abandoned connection keeps its socket AND its `maxReconnectAttempts: -1` reconnect loop forever; `disconnect()` only ever closes the most recent one. Neither fail-fast nor idempotent — the seam gives no hint that a second `connect()` silently strands a live link.
failure: Live against nats:2.10-alpine: `const p = new NatsPlugin(); await p.connect(cfg); await p.connect(cfg); await p.disconnect();` — `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` reports two `TCPSocketWrap` handles and the process never exits (still alive 3 s later). The single-connect control reports one handle and exits 0.
remediation: Either close/drain the previous `nc` at the top of `connect()` (i.e. call the teardown path first), or throw `already connected — call disconnect() first`. Silently abandoning a live link with an unbounded reconnect loop is the one option that leaves no diagnosable trace.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a lifecycle table over seam-call sequences — connect/connect, connect/disconnect/connect, connect/subscribe/connect, disconnect-without-connect, disconnect/disconnect — asserting for each that after the final `disconnect()` no NATS socket remains (`process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` holds no `TCPSocketWrap`, or a live `$SYS` CONNZ count returns to baseline) and no server-side consumer remains. Existing recovery.test.ts only covers connect/disconnect/connect, which is the one ordering that happens to be safe.

summary: `streamName()` composes `stream_prefix + safeName(topic)` with no length check, but JetStream caps a stream name at 255 bytes. Every other name-composition failure in this plugin is refused at `connect()` naming the field the operator can change (`validatePrefix` goes to some length to do exactly that, including composing a PROBE_TOKEN to judge the composed name), and `safeName` throws a named error when the fold rewrites its own output — but length falls through to a raw driver error that names neither the topic nor `stream_prefix`. Reachable with a caller-supplied topic via `post_topics`, and with an operator-supplied long `stream_prefix` that `connect()` happily accepts.
failure: Live: `plugin.post('x'.repeat(300), 'sys', 'hi')` -> `NatsError: stream name is too long, maximum allowed is 255`. Same for `fetchRecent` on that topic. The message mentions neither the topic string nor `stream_prefix`, so an operator whose 250-char `stream_prefix` passed `connect()` cleanly sees a first-post failure pointing at nothing they wrote.
remediation: Add a length bound to the composed name: reject an over-long `stream_prefix` at `connect()` (validatePrefix already composes a probe name — bound its length there), and raise a plugin error from `streamName()` naming the topic, the composed name, its length and the 255 limit when the topic pushes it over.
testUpgrade: Extend config.test.ts's `composedCases` table — which today only varies separator placement — with a LENGTH axis: for each of {prefix short/at-limit/over-limit} x {topic short/at-limit/over-limit}, assert either acceptance or a rejection whose message contains the offending field name (`stream_prefix` or the topic string). Assert the boundary exactly (255 and 256) so an off-by-one in whatever bound is added is caught, and add the same axis for `subject_prefix`/subject length.

summary: The push loop paces only an EMPTY events answer; any answer carrying a non-empty `events` array that neither delivers a message nor advances `lastEventId` is graded healthy, so the loop re-polls immediately forever — a silent ~1500 req/s flood against the operator's Zulip, with nothing on stderr.
failure: Subscribe to a topic, then have /api/v1/events answer every poll with a body the loop cannot ack. Measured in-process against the fake: `{result:'success',events:[{id:1,type:'heartbeat'}]}` -> 2316 polls in 2s; `events:[null]` -> 3019; `events:[7]` -> 3800; `events:[{id:'a',type:'message',message:{...}}]` -> 3968. All four report 0 `[parley-zulip]` stderr lines and never back off. Three of the four are shapes the package's own MALFORMED_EVENTS table already enumerates as reachable wire shapes, and `pollForWake` (line 520) explicitly paces exactly this case on the dedicated-queue path ("a poll answered at once with a heartbeat ... is a wake that never came"). The README asserts the opposite for the loop: "a server answering neither is reported on stderr and backed off rather than polled forever".
remediation: In `advance()`, make the health test "the answer moved something", not "the answer was non-empty": after the event scan, if `!sawMessage && lastEventId` did not advance (and the poll was `parked`), treat it as a non-event and go through `backoff('an events poll answered without advancing the queue')` instead of `recovered()`. A real heartbeat carries a fresh event id and so still advances `lastEventId`, which keeps a healthy idle queue off the failure path — the same discriminator `pollForWake` already uses.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a server answer that is not a delivery must be paced and reported", not the heartbeat instance. Add a `persistent` axis to operability.test.ts's PERMANENT_FAILURES table and populate it from the shared FAULTS vocabulary plus push-loop-containment's MALFORMED_EVENTS (heartbeatOnly, [null], [7], numeric/string event ids, message event with a non-numeric `id`), injected with `times` OMITTED so the fault persists; assert the existing `hot >= 10` bound on every LOOP_ROUTE and a non-empty `[parley-zulip]` stderr report. Widen fixture-hygiene's "every FAULTS entry is used" lint to "every FAULTS entry is used on BOTH the blocked-fetch path and the push-loop path", so a shape covered on one path cannot stay uncovered on its mirror.

summary: Every malformed-events row injects the fault with `times: 1`, so the table grades survival-and-recovery but can never grade pacing; the two fault tables partition the fault vocabulary such that no shape is graded on both axes, which is why the flood above ships as covered.
failure: push-loop-containment.test.ts injects each of its 7 MALFORMED_EVENTS shapes once (`{ status: 200, body: fault.body, times: 1 }`) and then asserts the loop recovers — a loop that hot-spins for one request looks identical to one that paces. operability.test.ts's PERMANENT_FAILURES table does inject persistently and does assert the rate bound, but its rows are only emptyBody / unparseableEvents / status codes / hangs; FAULTS.heartbeatOnly appears nowhere in it (it is used only in blocking-fetch.test.ts's DEGRADATIONS). testUpgrade: Add a self-test beside fixture-hygiene's existing vocabulary lint: for every key of FAULTS, assert it appears in at least one PERSISTENT push-loop row and one transient row, failing with the fault name when a shape is graded on only one axis.
