summary: `MIN_EVENTS_TIMEOUT_MS = 250` is documented as the safe floor ("no value can make the loop poll hot"), but each cap costs TWO requests (the capped parked poll plus the `dont_block=true` probe after it), so the documented minimum sustains 460 polls/minute PER SUBSCRIBED TOPIC against a server whose documented default limit — cited in this package's own test comments — is 200 requests/minute per user.
failure: connect({ events_timeout_ms: 250 }) + subscribe(one topic), server parks longer than the cap (the normal healthy idle case): measured 23 polls in 3s = 460/min for ONE topic, 100/min at events_timeout_ms=1000, 20/min at the 25000 default. Two topics at 1000ms, or one at 250ms, already exceed Zulip's default per-user budget, putting the bridge in permanent 429 backoff — while README's config table says the clamp exists "so no value can make the loop poll hot" and config.test.ts's SANE_REQUEST_CEILING of 20-per-800ms passes it.
remediation: Either raise the floor to a value whose 2-requests-per-cap rate is under the server's documented budget with headroom for several topics (a few seconds), or stop spending a second request per cap — only issue the `dont_block=true` liveness probe after a cap that is SUSPICIOUS (e.g. the second consecutive capped park), so a healthy idle poll costs one request per cap. Whichever is chosen, state the resulting per-topic request rate in the README rather than the unqualified "cannot poll hot".
testUpgrade: Turn config.test.ts's SANE_REQUEST_CEILING into a rate budget parameterized over `events_timeout_ms` AND topic count: for each of {min, 1000, default} x {1, 4} subscribed topics, assert total requests/minute stays under a named `ZULIP_DEFAULT_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN` constant declared next to SERVER_CONSTRAINTS. That guards the class (a config bound that is legal locally but illegal against the server) instead of today's flat 20-requests-per-800ms, which no floor can fail.

summary: The seam-mapping table says a bad URL surfaces on the first CALL; the config section forty lines later, and the code, reject it at `connect()`. Two claims in one README disagree about when a misconfiguration fails.
failure: `connect({ site_url: 'not-a-url' })` rejects immediately with "backend_config.site_url must be an absolute http(s) URL" (requireHttpUrl, line 1287; pinned by config.test.ts's site_url rows). An operator reading the table row "connect captures config; a bad URL/key surfaces on the first call" expects the bridge to come up and fail at the first post — the opposite of the fail-fast behaviour the package actually implements and the Config section documents.
remediation: Reword the table row to distinguish the two: a MALFORMED site_url or an empty email/api_key/stream is a `connect()` error; a well-formed URL pointing at the wrong host, or a wrong-but-well-formed api_key, is what surfaces on the first request (401).
testUpgrade: Extend the README-vs-code lint the package already runs in spirit (comment-hygiene's README duplication check) with a claims test: extract the README's Config table key names and, for each, assert that a deliberately invalid value of that key is rejected by `connect()` — driven off DECLARED_CONFIG_KEYS so the rows widen with the config surface. That guards the class "a doc sentence states the wrong failure TIME" rather than this one sentence.

summary: The gateway socket is opened at the bare URL `GET /gateway/bot` returns, with none of Discord's REQUIRED `?v=` / `?encoding=` query-string params appended. Discord's gateway documents `v` and `encoding` as required; the URL handed back by `/gateway/bot` is `wss://gateway.discord.gg/` with no params, so the plugin dials an unversioned gateway on every real deployment.
failure: Live config `{ token: <real bot token> }` (no `gateway_url` override). `resolveGatewayUrl()` returns `wss://gateway.discord.gg/`; `dial()` passes it verbatim to `new WebSocket(url)` — traced at src/index.ts:781-784 and 786-789, and `grep -rn 'encoding=json|v=10' packages/bridge-discord` returns nothing. Discord resolves an unversioned connect to a decommissioned API version and closes with 4012, which is in TERMINAL_CLOSE (src/index.ts:136) → `fatalGateway` is set, the reconnect ladder stops, and `subscribe` rejects with TerminalGatewayCloseError. push-loop.ts:68 rethrows anything that is not NoSuchTopicError and stdio-bridge.ts:155 tears the bridge down, so `createStdioBridge` rejects and cli.ts exits 1 — a correctly-provisioned bot never starts, and the stderr line blames "the bot token and the MESSAGE CONTENT privileged intent". No test sees it: gateway-reconnect.test.ts:645 asserts `expect(first.url).toBe('ws://first')`, pinning the omission. I verified this by mutating dial() to append `?v=10&encoding=json` — 32 cases went red purely on URL equality, i.e. the suite locks the non-conformant URL in rather than checking it.
remediation: Append the required params in `dial()` before `openSocket`, preserving any the resolved/overridden URL already carries: parse with `new URL(base)`, set `v=10` and `encoding=json` on `searchParams`, and dial the result. Keep the fakes honest by having `FakeWs`/the fake gateway REFUSE a connect URL without `v=10&encoding=json`, the same way they already refuse an IDENTIFY without the token or the intent bits.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a vendor wire obligation carried on the CONNECT URL rather than in a frame — invisible to a fake that accepts any URL. Parameterize a table over `[gateway_url override, url resolved via GET /gateway/bot]` x `[base with no query, base with a trailing slash, base that already carries ?v=10, base carrying an unrelated param]`, asserting on the dialed URL that `v` and `encoding` are present exactly once and that pre-existing params survive. Make the enforcement load-bearing: have `fake-gateway.ts`'s constructor and `fake-discord.ts`'s WebSocketServer `connection` handler reject a URL missing either param (a `4012`-shaped close), so the plugin cannot silently stop sending them. gateway-reconnect.test.ts:637 ('re-resolves the gateway url on every attempt') is the existing test too narrow to catch this — it compares the dialed URL to the raw resolved string.

summary: Two gateway protocol obligations are implemented but wholly unexercised: the op 1 HEARTBEAT-REQUEST branch and the `s` sequence tracking. Both can be deleted and the entire 568-case suite stays green, so they are counted as coverage while being untested.
failure: Mutation 1: `case OP.HEARTBEAT: { ws.send(JSON.stringify({ op: OP.HEARTBEAT, d: this.seq })); break; }` (src/index.ts:917-920) → `case OP.HEARTBEAT: { break; }`. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-discord` → 15 files passed, 568/568 tests passed. Mutation 2: delete `if (typeof payload.s === 'number') this.seq = payload.s;` (src/index.ts:887) → 568/568 passed. Against real Discord, mutation 1 means the client never answers the gateway's request for an immediate heartbeat, so the connection is zombied and closed (op 1 is exactly how Discord probes a socket it suspects is dead), and every long-poll waiter and every subscription on that socket dies with it — silently, on a schedule only the provider controls. Neither fake ever sends an op 1, and neither inspects the `d` of a client heartbeat.
remediation: Make the fakes enforce the obligations they model: in `fake-gateway.ts` and `fake-discord.ts`, add a server-initiated op 1 and close the socket (4009-shaped) if the client does not answer with an op 1 within one interval, and assert the heartbeat's `d` echoes the last dispatch `s` the server sent. Keep the enforcement AHEAD of the scriptable `state.onIdentify` hook, as the token/intent checks already are.
testUpgrade: CLASS: 'a gateway obligation only the real provider punishes'. Add a parameterized table over the SERVER-INITIATED opcodes and state the plugin owes an answer to — `[op 1 heartbeat request, op 11 ack withheld, op 7 RECONNECT, op 9 INVALID_SESSION]` x `[before READY, after READY, on a superseded socket]` — where the fake gateway CLOSES the socket when the obligation is not met, so a deleted branch loses a case. Cross it with a `d`-value axis asserting the client heartbeat echoes the last dispatched `s` (send dispatches with s=1,2,3 and assert the next op 1 carries `d: 3`, and `d: null` on a socket that has dispatched nothing). This is the same class as the gateway-URL finding above: the fakes accept anything the plugin happens to send at the transport layer.

summary: `api_url` and `gateway_url` are accepted verbatim with no scheme check, so an operator who points either at a plaintext non-loopback endpoint ships the bot token in the clear with no warning — a class this repo already guards in bridge-matrix, bridge-xmpp, bridge-zulip and bridge-telegram.
failure: `connect({ token: 'REAL_BOT_TOKEN', api_url: 'http://proxy.internal/api/v10', gateway_url: 'ws://proxy.internal' })` is accepted silently (src/index.ts:287-289; the only validation applied is a trailing-slash strip). Every REST call then sends `Authorization: Bot REAL_BOT_TOKEN` over cleartext HTTP (src/index.ts:1025) and the gateway IDENTIFY sends `{ token: REAL_BOT_TOKEN }` over cleartext WS (src/index.ts:878). Compare `packages/bridge-matrix/src/index.ts:177-182`, which warns on exactly this shape for `homeserver_url` and is anchored by a test. Discord token compromise is high-blast-radius: the same token is shared across every bridge instance per this package's own README.
remediation: Reuse matrix's `plaintextRemoteOrigin` shape (extract it to `bridge-net-util` rather than copying it): at `connect()`, warn on stderr when `api_url` is `http://` or `gateway_url` is `ws://` to any non-loopback host, naming the origin and the credential at risk. Keep it a warning, not a rejection, so the in-process fakes and loopback dev setups still work.
testUpgrade: CLASS: 'a configurable endpoint that carries a secret and accepts a plaintext scheme'. Add a table over `[api_url, gateway_url]` x `[https/wss remote (silent), http/ws loopback 127.0.0.1 (silent), http/ws ::1 (silent), http/ws IPv4-mapped loopback (silent), http/ws remote hostname (warns), http/ws remote IP (warns)]`, asserting the warning names the offending key and origin and that no warning fires for the safe rows. This is worth lifting into a shared net-util test helper so every HTTP/WS backend runs the identical table — bridge-slack has the same gap.

summary: The `subscribe` row argues at length that a per-topic failure must not fail core's attach "because failing here would fail core's attach and take the REST half of the bridge down with it" — then describes a terminal close as merely "stops the loop, is reported on stderr, and makes later gateway calls fail fast", never saying that a terminal close on the FIRST subscribe does exactly the thing the paragraph warns against.
failure: A bot whose MESSAGE CONTENT privileged intent was never toggled (the step the README itself flags as easy to miss) gets gateway close 4013/4014. Traced: openSocket's close handler builds a TerminalGatewayCloseError (src/index.ts:958-964) → `subscribe` rethrows it (src/index.ts:591-594) → push-loop.ts:68 rethrows anything that is not NoSuchTopicError → stdio-bridge.ts:155 sets toreDown, calls releaseAll() and rethrows → `createStdioBridge` rejects → cli.ts:53 prints fatal and `process.exit(1)`. The bridge will not start at all, even though the REST half (post, fetchRecent, resolveIdentity) needs no gateway intent and would work perfectly. A reader of the README expects the same stderr-and-carry-on treatment the surrounding text promises. (The behaviour itself was adjudicated in round 4 — this is only about the documentation of its cost.)
remediation: State it in the `subscribe` row and in the provisioning callout: a terminal gateway close (4004 / 4010-4014) raised while the first subscribe is attaching fails core's attach and the bridge exits — the operator symptom is `parley-discord: fatal: …` at startup, not an idle bridge — and name the fix per code (token, MESSAGE CONTENT toggle). If the intent is instead that catch-up should survive it, that is a behaviour change, not a doc change.
testUpgrade: CLASS: 'a README that documents the isolation rule but not the case that breaks it'. readme.test.ts already asserts README prose against real constants; extend that pattern to BEHAVIOUR: a table over `[transient close 1006, handshake stall, gateway-url lookup 500, terminal 4004, terminal 4012, terminal 4014]` driving `startPushLoop` through core, asserting for each row both the observed outcome (attach resolves vs attach rejects) AND that the README contains a sentence naming that outcome for that class of close. A row whose behaviour and prose disagree fails.

summary: MENTION_RE backtracks quadratically on attacker-controlled Slack `text`, so one ordinary-length message stalls the whole single-threaded bridge for seconds and a page of them for over a minute.
failure: Anyone who can post in a mapped channel sends a 40 000-char message of '<@' repeated 20 000 times (Slack's own text limit is 40 000, so this is a legal post). `renderMentions` runs `/<([@!])([^>|\s]*)(?:\|([^>]*))?>/g` over it: `[^>|\s]*` swallows the tail, finds no `>` or `|`, and backtracks one character at a time, once per '<' start position. Reproduced through the plugin: `fetchRecent` over ONE such history entry took 1664 ms; over a single 50-entry page it took 77 490 ms of fully blocked event loop. During that block no Socket Mode ack is flushed, so Slack redelivers and eventually drops the connection, and every other topic, the presence loop and the MCP stdio server are frozen with it. The same rewrite runs on the live path inside `ws.on('message')`, so the push path is stalled identically. Measured growth is quadratic: 4k chars 18 ms, 8k 62 ms, 16k 243 ms, 32k 987 ms.
remediation: Bound the input before the rewrite and make the pattern non-backtracking. Cheapest correct fix: refuse to run `renderMentions` on `text` longer than a stated ceiling (return it verbatim), and rewrite MENTION_RE so the body class excludes `<` as well as `>`/`|`/whitespace, which removes the overlapping start positions that produce the quadratic term. Core already states this policy for regexes it did not author (`regex-safety.ts`: MAX_MATCH_INPUT with 'Callers MUST clamp or refuse longer input'); this call site is the same hazard with a fixed pattern and unbounded input.
testUpgrade: Parameterize an adversarial-text corpus rather than pinning the one string: rows = {repeated '<@', repeated '<!', repeated '<@x|', repeated '<#', one unterminated '<@' + 40k filler, 40k of '&'} crossed with lengths {1k, 10k, 40k} and driven through BOTH the history walk and the live push path, each asserting per-message wall clock under a bound (e.g. 50 ms) and that the socket still acks afterwards. Widen `hostile-input.test.ts`'s BAD_ENTRIES generator to include a `text` axis — today it only varies `ts`, `user`/`bot_id` and entry shape, so no row in the suite ever hands the plugin a long text at all. The class is 'a vendor-markup rewrite applied to unbounded untrusted text', so the same table should be inherited by the next transport with its own markup.

summary: `handshake_timeout_ms` and `rotation_grace_ms` are read straight out of `backend_config` into `setTimeout`, so an out-of-range value silently clamps to 1 ms and disables the feature the knob exists to bound.
failure: `backend_config: { handshake_timeout_ms: 2147483648 }` (a plausible 'give it a month' figure). Node clamps the delay to 1 ms and warns on stderr, so the handshake timer fires before `hello` can arrive: reproduced, `subscribe` rejects after 53 ms with `Error: Slack Socket Mode sent no hello within 2147483648ms` — an error naming a figure that never applied — and live push is permanently unavailable for the process, with every blocking `fetchRecent` silently degraded to the history ladder. `0`, `-1` and `NaN` reproduce the same outcome (12 ms / 9 ms / 7 ms). `rotation_grace_ms: 2147483648` reproduces the mirror image: the grace timer fires at 1 ms, so the old socket is closed before the replacement handshake completes and the zero-gap rotation DEFAULT_ROTATION_GRACE_MS exists to provide never happens — sampled 40 times over 1 s, `liveSockets` never reached 2. bridge-matrix already bounds exactly this class (`MAX_TIMER_MS = 2**31 - 1`, `MAX_SYNC_TIMEOUT_MS`, with the 'past it every one of them silently becomes 1ms' rationale) and rejects at load; bridge-slack validates its two string maps and neither number.
remediation: Extend the existing load-time validation (`requireUsableMap` / `requireUsableChannelMap`) with a numeric check for both knobs: reject unless `Number.isInteger(v) && v > 0 && v <= 2**31 - 1`, naming the key and the accepted range, the way matrix's `validateConfig` does. Fail at `connect`, not at first use — an unusable timing knob taking effect in a shape nothing else expects is the same defect class as `skip_permissions: true`.
testUpgrade: Add a table over EVERY numeric/timing key in `SlackBackendConfig` (today `handshake_timeout_ms`, `rotation_grace_ms`; the row list must be derived from the interface so a new knob cannot be added without a row) crossed with the unusable-value corpus already used for the string maps: [0, -1, 1.5, NaN, Infinity, 2**31, 2**53, '10000', null, {}]. Assert `connect` rejects naming the key and the range. Mirror the existing `UNUSABLE_TARGETS` block in `hostile-input.test.ts`, which covers `channel_map`/`mention_map` values and is exactly the shape needed here.

summary: `api_url` is accepted without any validation or warning, so a config pointing it at a plaintext or third-party host ships the `xoxb-`/`xapp-` tokens there in the clear, silently — while every other backend in the repo warns at connect.
failure: `backend_config: { api_url: 'http://logger.internal.example/api', bot_token: 'xoxb-…', app_token: 'xapp-…' }`. Every Web API call then POSTs `Authorization: Bearer xoxb-…` unencrypted to that host, and `apps.connections.open` does the same with the app token; nothing is printed and nothing fails, so the operator has no signal at all. `api_url: 42` is worse in a different direction: `cfg.api_url.replace` throws `TypeError: cfg.api_url.replace is not a function` from inside `connect`, naming neither the key nor the plugin. Grepping `packages/bridge-slack/src/` for warn/stderr returns nothing outside `cli.ts`; bridge-matrix (`configRisks` / `plaintextRemoteOrigin` / `isLoopbackHost`), bridge-redis, bridge-xmpp, bridge-postgres and bridge-sqlite all emit connect-time config-risk warnings. Slack is the one backend with a fully configurable credentialed endpoint and no such path.
remediation: Validate `api_url` at load (non-empty string, parses as an http(s) URL — reject otherwise, naming the key), and emit a connect-time warning when it is `http://` to a non-loopback host, stating that the bot and app tokens cross the network in the clear. Reuse matrix's `plaintextRemoteOrigin`/`isLoopbackHost` shape rather than a prefix match, so a DNS name like `127.0.0.1.example.com` is still warned about.
testUpgrade: One shared table, applied per backend that takes a credentialed URL from `backend_config`: rows = {https remote, http loopback (127.x, ::1, localhost), http remote, http DNS-name-shaped-like-loopback, non-URL string, non-string} × assert(load rejects | warns naming the key | is silent). Slack's rows would be new; matrix's existing plaintext test is the template. Grading it as a table over backends is what stops the theme reappearing in the next transport under a fresh key name (`api_url`, `homeserver_url`, `base_url`, …).

summary: Each rung of the blocking-fetch ladder re-runs a full `conversations.history` walk from the caller's original `since`, so ordinary unsurfaced traffic above the cursor multiplies the per-call request count by the backlog — the poll-storm ceiling the suite and README both state is only true when nothing unsurfaced sits above the floor.
failure: A channel with 300 `channel_join` records above the stored cursor (entirely ordinary traffic; the same holds for plain thread replies), Socket Mode unavailable, `blockMs = 3000`. Reproduced: the ladder has 4 rungs, `blocking-fetch.test.ts` asserts `hits('conversations.history') <= rungs + 2 = 6`, and the README states '4 + block_ms / MAX_DIAL_BACKOFF_MS reads — 16 reads and dials at the default 60 s' — the actual count was 30. Each rung walks to cursor exhaustion (6 pages) and throws the position away, because `blockForMessage` keeps passing the caller's original `args`. Scaled to the defaults (60 s budget = 16 rungs) over a few thousand unsurfaced records, one blocked `fetch_recent` is ~240 `conversations.history` requests on one channel — on the 1-request-per-minute tier the README itself documents, that is hours of a single tool call. The existing ceiling cannot fail on this because every row it runs uses a channel with at most one entry above the floor.
remediation: Carry the walk's own progress across rungs: after an empty re-query, advance the local floor used for the next rung (and for newly armed waiters) to `requeried.nextCursor`, which is monotone and already the position the walk proved it read to; return that same highest-reached cursor from the `aborted` path instead of the caller's original `since`. That collapses N rungs over a backlog to one walk plus N-1 single-page reads and also removes the pointless re-read latency.
testUpgrade: Widen the DEGRADATIONS/poll-storm tables in `blocking-fetch.test.ts` with a second axis they currently fix at zero: the number of UNSURFACED entries above `since` (rows 0, 50, 300, 1000, using the `channel_join` and thread-reply shapes `catchup-window.test.ts` already builds). The ceiling must stay `rungs + k` independent of that axis. Same axis belongs on the README cost claim in `documented-scopes.test.ts`, so the prose figure and the executable bound move together. The class is 'per-call work bounded by wall clock for one input shape only' — it should be asserted against a backlog dimension, not a single-message fixture.

summary: `resolveIdentity`'s `auth.test` branch — the memoized network call and the id it returns — is graded by nothing: replacing its result with a passthrough leaves the whole suite green.
failure: Mutation: `return { handle, backendRef: auth.user_id ?? handle }` → `return { handle, backendRef: handle }`. Result: 504/504 tests pass (14 files). The only test that drives this branch, `connection-lifecycle.test.ts`'s `authTestPromise / auth.test ok:false` row, calls `plugin.resolveIdentity(asHandle('parley-bot'))` purely to count wire hits and never inspects the returned `BackendIdentity`. So the README claim 'own bot name → `auth.test` user id' (README.md line 21) is unbacked, the `handle === auth.user || handle === auth.user_id` discrimination is unbacked, and the branch could resolve the bot to anything — or be deleted outright — without the suite noticing. The fake serves `{ user: 'parley-bot', user_id: 'U0PARLEY' }`, so the discriminating assertion is one line away and simply is not made.
remediation: No source change needed for the mutation itself; add the missing assertions. If the branch turns out to have no consumer of `backendRef`, that is the finding to act on instead — delete it and the `auth.test` call, and drop the row from the README scope table.
testUpgrade: A parameterized `resolveIdentity` outcome table — the seam method with the most branches and the least grading — with rows {handle containing '@' that resolves, '@' handle that is users_not_found, '@' handle on missing_scope, the bot's `user` name, the bot's `user_id`, an unrelated bare handle, a handle equal to neither but sharing a prefix} × asserted `{handle, backendRef}` pairs. `http-contract.test.ts` already owns the '@' rows for error mapping but asserts `backendRef` only there; the bare-handle rows are the gap. Guard the class 'a seam method whose returned value no row asserts' by requiring each seam method to have at least one row asserting its full return shape.

summary: Two waiter-lifecycle guards whose comments claim they are load-bearing can both be deleted with the suite staying green: nothing in 504 tests observes the waiter registry.
failure: Mutation A: delete `wake();` before `return requeried;` in `blockForMessage` (line 398) — the satisfied long-poll's waiter stays registered, with its timer live, for up to one ladder rung (5 s) after the call has returned; every live event on that channel then iterates stale waiters. Mutation B: delete `this.drainWaiters();` from the socket `close` handler (line 737), whose comment states 'Keep the loss of an ESTABLISHED socket calling this, so that a caller parked on a stream that has stopped serving falls back to the history ladder instead of holding its whole budget on a dead socket'. Both mutations applied together: 504/504 green. Mutation B is green because the rung timer, not `drainWaiters`, is what actually bounds the park — and the only row that could see the difference (`an established socket dropped mid-park`, blockMs 4000 with rungs at 0/500/1500/3500) is bounded by the rung well inside its tolerance. So the comment overstates the guarantee AND the guarantee is untested.
remediation: Expose the waiter-registry size (or assert it through an existing observable) and pin it. Then either raise the DEGRADATIONS budget so `drainWaiters` is the thing being measured, or downgrade the comment to state what is actually true — that the rung bound is the guarantee and the drain is a latency optimisation.
testUpgrade: A registry-hygiene invariant asserted after EVERY blocking-fetch row, not a new point test: once each `fetchRecent({blockMs})` settles (returned, rejected, or was aborted by `disconnect()`), the plugin holds zero registered waiters and zero pending waiter timers. Drive it as an `afterEach` over the existing STAGES / ELIGIBILITY / DEGRADATIONS tables so it covers wake, timeout, disconnect and socket-loss exits together. Add one DEGRADATIONS row with `blockMs` large enough that a rung is already at MAX_DIAL_BACKOFF_MS (e.g. 20 000) and the message lands just after a mid-park socket drop, so the drain-vs-rung difference becomes observable latency.

summary: `connect()` resets some instance state and silently keeps the rest, so a second `connect()` without a `disconnect()` leaves the previous session's routes, socket, memoized auth and reconnect loop running under the new configuration.
failure: `connect(cfgA); subscribe('C0A', handlerA); connect(cfgB); post('C0A', …)` — reproduced: `handlerA` still fires ('stale route fired: ["after re-connect"]') on the socket opened under cfgA, and `fake.liveSockets` shows the old socket was never closed. `connect` clears `channelOwner` but not `routes`, `sockets`, `ws`, `wsReady`, `waiters`, `authTestPromise`, `reconnecting` or `rotating` — so the new session inherits the old session's channel→handler map and its `auth.test` answer for a possibly different `bot_token`. Same class, second shape: `disconnect()` sets `stopped` but leaves a `reconnect()` loop parked in `await delay(<=5000)`; a `connect()` inside that window flips `stopped` back to false, the loop resumes, and it dials `apps.connections.open` and opens a socket the new session never asked for and no `subscribe` is behind. Neither shape is exercised — `connection-lifecycle.test.ts`'s 'stale route' row always calls `disconnect()` first.
remediation: Make the boundary explicit rather than half-reset: either reject a second `connect()` while `this.connected` (fail-fast, matching the repo's no-silent-no-op stance), or have `connect()` perform the full `disconnect()` teardown first. Also clear `reconnecting` (and abandon the loop) in `disconnect()` so a later `connect()` cannot resurrect it.
testUpgrade: A lifecycle state-machine table over the seam methods rather than a point test: for each state transition {cold→connect, connected→connect, connected→disconnect→connect, connected→disconnect→connect-inside-the-reconnect-backoff-window}, assert (a) sockets held by the plugin, (b) which handlers fire on a post, (c) whether a dial occurred, (d) that a memoized `auth.test` from the previous config is not reused. The 'disconnect from the {cold, establishing, established, rotating} state closes every socket' table in `connection-lifecycle.test.ts` is the right shape — this adds `connect` as a second transition axis, which guards the class 'lifecycle field the new entry point forgot to reset' rather than the two fields found today.

summary: unwrapEnvelope embeds an untrusted upstream body verbatim (sanitized, never redacted), so a body that echoes the request URL puts the bot token into the thrown error — i.e. into model context and the operator's logs.
failure: With the fake answering sendMessage HTTP 200 `{"ok":false,"description":"Bad Request from upstream http://127.0.0.1:35833/bottest-token/sendMessage"}`, `post()` rejects with `Telegram POST /sendMessage → ok:false: Bad Request from upstream http://127.0.0.1:35833/bottest-token/sendMessage` — the full credential-bearing URL, reproduced in a scratch test. net-util redacts exactly this on the status/transport paths (`errorBody`/`fetchOnce` call `redactUrls`), but a 2xx envelope never reaches those paths, and the plugin's own quoting only calls `sanitizeBody`. The same body also reaches stderr via `report()` from the poll loop and from chatIdFor's unresolved-topic diagnostic. The class doc for unwrapEnvelope names 'a rejecting middlebox or a non-conforming local Bot API server' as its motivating case — the same actor that echoes request lines.
remediation: Redact before quoting: either export net-util's `redactUrls`/a `redactSecrets(text, url)` helper and call it in `unwrapEnvelope` (it already has the label; pass the URL through), or, cheaper and local, have `TelegramPlugin.call` strip `this.token` and its percent-encoded spelling from any message it throws or reports. Do it at the single quoting choke point so no future error path can regress.
testUpgrade: Parameterized 'no diagnostic ever carries the credential' table: rows = each way an upstream can fail (2xx ok:false description, 2xx with no result, non-JSON 2xx body, 4xx/5xx status body, transport stall) x columns = each seam call (connect/post/fetchRecent/subscribe/resolveIdentity) plus the poll loop's stderr. Each cell makes the fake echo `${url}/bot${token}/<method>` into its body and asserts the rejection message AND every captured stderr line contain neither the raw token nor `encodeURIComponent(token)`, with a positive control asserting the fake really received the token so the guard cannot pass vacuously. Existing envelope.test.ts covers the shapes but never asserts on the token.

summary: `api_url` is accepted with no scheme check and no warning, so an http:// base URL ships the bot token — which this API carries in the URL PATH — across the network in the clear, while three sibling backends warn on exactly this config shape.
failure: `backend_config.api_url: 'http://bot-api.internal.example:8081'` (the documented 'local Bot API server' override, pointed at another host) makes every request `GET http://bot-api.internal.example:8081/bot<TOKEN>/getUpdates` — the full bot token in a cleartext request line, visible to any on-path observer and logged by every intermediate proxy. `connect()` succeeds silently; grep of packages/bridge-telegram/src shows no `protocol`/`URL(` check anywhere. bridge-matrix (`plaintextRemoteOrigin`, configRisks), bridge-zulip and bridge-xmpp all emit a SECURITY warning for the same shape, and the Telegram case is strictly worse because the credential is in the URL rather than in a header body.
remediation: Add the house-standard check to `connect`: parse `api_url`, and when the scheme is http: and the host is not loopback, write one SECURITY line to stderr naming the origin and saying the bot token rides the URL path in the clear. Reuse the sibling backends' `plaintextRemoteOrigin`/`isLoopbackHost` (lift them into parley-net-util rather than a fourth copy). Consider also refusing userinfo/query/fragment in `api_url`, as bridge-zulip's `requireHttpUrl` does, since both smuggle the token somewhere it is not expected.
testUpgrade: One shared parameterized table (in net-util's suite, re-run per backend that takes a base URL): rows = https remote, http://127.0.0.1, http://localhost, http://[::1], http://127.0.0.1.example.com, http://remote.example, https with userinfo; assertion = a SECURITY stderr line naming the ORIGIN appears iff the credential would cross the network unencrypted, and connect still succeeds. Telegram's row set must include the default (no api_url) as a negative control.

summary: `Subscription.watermark` and its `if (rec.seq <= sub.watermark) continue` can never fire — ingest only runs for freshly appended records, whose store-wide sequence exceeds every sequence stamped before the subscribe — yet a 7-line comment presents the watermark as what implements 'history is owned by catch-up, not push'.
failure: Mutation: `watermark: store.maxSeq(chatId)` -> `watermark: 0` leaves inbound.test.ts, guarantees.test.ts and conformance.test.ts fully green (124 passed). Instrumenting the branch to log when it fires and running the entire package suite (466 passed / 3 skipped) produced zero hits. So the field, the comparison and the comment are all inert: a future maintainer who changes ingest to replay history to a new subscriber will believe the watermark protects them, and it does not.
remediation: Delete `Subscription.watermark` and the guard, and move the real reason into the ingest doc: the once-only property comes from `store.append` returning undefined for anything already observed, so ingest is only ever called for records newer than any subscribe point. If the guard is wanted as defence for a future replay path, it must come with a test that fails when it is removed.
testUpgrade: Ratchet the class, not the field: a lint/mutation cell asserting that deleting each defensive branch in ingest/fetchRecent turns some test red (i.e. every guard is executed at least once), plus a push-ordering property test — subscribe at an arbitrary history depth, then interleave own posts and deferred foreign messages, and assert the subscriber receives exactly the records admitted after subscribe, in ascending sequence, none earlier.

summary: The fake forcibly stamps `update_id` on every injected update, so the poll loop's documented NaN-poison protection (acknowledge only an update that states an id) is unexercised and can be deleted with the suite green.
failure: `injectRawUpdate(payload)` builds `{ ...payload, update_id: updateSeq++ }` — update_id last, so a test that passes `{update_id: undefined}` or `{update_id: 'x'}` gets a valid numeric one anyway, and `injectRaw`/`injectUserMessage(Deferred)` never expose the field at all. Consequently the branch at src/index.ts:663 (`typeof u?.update_id === 'number' && Number.isFinite(...)`) has no reachable failing input in this suite: removing the guard, so that one id-less update sets `offset = NaN` and re-serves the whole backlog forever at the idle floor, keeps every test green — including the cadence table that exists to catch exactly 'a batch re-served forever'.
remediation: Let the fake emit a non-conforming update: give `injectRawUpdate` an escape hatch that does not overwrite a caller-supplied `update_id` (or add `injectMalformedUpdate`). Then add rows for missing / non-numeric / NaN / Infinity update_id.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing CADENCE_CELLS table with an upstream-conformance axis: for each of {no update_id, string update_id, NaN, Infinity, negative} mixed into a batch with valid updates, assert (a) the valid updates are ingested exactly once, (b) `offset` still advances — measured as the fake's retainedUpdates() dropping to 0 — and (c) the poll count stays under the same handful-per-second bound. That guards the class 'a non-conforming upstream field poisons the acknowledgement protocol', not just this one field.

summary: `requireMessage` accepts any finite `date`, so an out-of-range value survives validation and blows up later as `RangeError: Invalid time value` — the contextless diagnostic its own JSDoc says the check exists to prevent — and the update is dropped and acknowledged.
failure: Injecting a message with `date: 1e15` (finite, in range for Number, out of range for Date) produces exactly one stderr line: `parley-telegram: dropped update 1: Invalid time value` — naming neither the endpoint nor the field, while the message is permanently lost (the update was acknowledged to Telegram before ingest ran, and there is no history endpoint). Reproduced. The same value on the `sendMessage` response makes `post` reject with the 'Telegram accepted it and the store did not record it' error whose stated cause is wrong.
remediation: Validate the field for what it is used for: require `Number.isFinite(msg.date)` AND that `new Date(msg.date * 1000)` is a valid time (e.g. `Math.abs(msg.date) <= 8.64e12/1000`), and throw `${label}: message carries an out-of-range date` so the diagnostic names the endpoint and the field like its siblings.
testUpgrade: Parameterized malformed-Message table x both ingest paths (getUpdates update, sendMessage response): {missing, null, string, NaN, Infinity, 1e15, -1e15} x {date, message_id, chat.id}, asserting for every cell that the diagnostic names the endpoint AND the field, and that the loop keeps consuming. That guards the class 'a field validated for type but not for domain resurfaces as an unlabelled runtime error' rather than the one date value.

summary: Every fixture in this package — the reference plugin, the throwing reference, and all 30 BROKEN_VARIANTS — is built by `context()`, which hard-codes `supportsBlockingFetch: false` and `carriesSenderIdentity: true`. No control ever takes the other arm, so every assertion that lives inside a capability-TRUE branch has no negative control at all: the whole native-blocking half of the suite (wake-on-message, cursor-advanced, empty-page-at-timeout, the ≥150ms 'it actually waited' bound) AND the entire true arm of the 0-3ms lost-wakeup race case can be deleted with this package fully green. The suite-shape self-check only demands that the FALSE arm asserts, and negative-control only demands one variant per CLAUSE — a clause whose control exercises the other arm satisfies both.
failure: Mutation: delete the bodies of both `if (!ctx.supportsBlockingFetch) {...return;}` cases' fall-through (native) arms in packages/conformance/src/index.ts, i.e. remove the (a)/(b) blocking assertions and the whole `pending = fetchRecent({since: tail, blockMs: 5000})` race arm. `npx vitest run packages/conformance` → 7 files, 303/303 passed, including negative-control's 67 rows. Eight backends that declare supportsBlockingFetch: true (redis, nats, matrix, postgres, xmpp, …) would then be certified while asserting nothing about blocking fetch or the lost-wakeup window — the repo's own stated richest defect vein.
remediation: Make the capability flags an axis of the control set, not a constant: give `context()` an override so BROKEN_VARIANTS can declare `supportsBlockingFetch: true` (an in-memory plugin that really honours blockMs is ~10 lines over the existing store) and `carriesSenderIdentity: false`, then add variants that break the native arm (a blocked read that returns at the budget rather than on the message; one that reports a moved cursor on an empty timeout; the park-from-now variant re-aimed at the true arm) and the false-identity arm (a plugin that blanks/scrambles senderHandle when identity is declared not carried).
testUpgrade: In negative-control.test.ts add a table derived from CONTEXT_FIELDS: for every boolean capability field × each of its two values, require at least one BROKEN_VARIANTS entry whose fixture declares that value AND whose mustFail clause is one that branches on the flag — so a new capability flag, or a new arm, arrives as a red row instead of as silently uncontrolled coverage. Pair it with a suite-shape row asserting that each capability-guarded case has BOTH arms covered by some fixture in this package (the existing 'gives `%s` a false arm that still asserts' row is too narrow: it only inspects source text, never whether anything runs the other side).

summary: 'disconnect is idempotent and stops the plugin serving' grades only that `post` rejects afterwards. Its second assertion, `expect(live).toHaveLength(1)`, cannot fail: nothing writes to the topic after teardown, so no plugin can grow `live`. The comment above it claims the live half 'needs a second, independent client the context cannot hand out yet' — but `concurrentPost` is exactly that independent client and is already required by the context and used by two other cases. DESIGN/seam declare disconnect tears down the connection AND all subscriptions; that half is ungraded.
failure: Probe (packages/conformance/test/probe-b.test.ts, run then removed): a plugin whose `disconnect()` only sets `torn = true` — it never unregisters its subscription, never stops the loop, and whose `cleanup` is a no-op — while `post` rejects when torn. `npx vitest run` → 32/32 conformance cases pass. Core would then keep receiving `<channel>` events for a torn-down backend and the MCP process cannot exit.
remediation: After the double `disconnect()`, when `ctx.concurrentPost !== 'unsupported'`, drive `await ctx.concurrentPost(t, 1, 1)`, wait a beat, and assert `live` is still length 1; also assert `fetchRecent` and `subscribe` reject after teardown (the seam's teardown covers reads and the live path, not just writes). Delete the stale comment rather than restating it. Add a BROKEN_VARIANTS entry per teardown responsibility (leaks the subscription; keeps serving reads).
testUpgrade: Parameterize teardown as a table over SEAM RESPONSIBILITIES — [post rejects, fetchRecent rejects, subscribe rejects, no further live delivery from an independent writer] — one row each, and add one BROKEN_VARIANTS entry per row so the negative control forces each to be failable. Guard the class generally with a self-check that flags any assertion in the suite made after a state-changing call with no intervening stimulus (here: `expect(live).toHaveLength(1)` with no writer between it and the earlier waitFor).

summary: `credentialParts` treats EVERY query value as a secret — no length floor beyond 2 characters and none of the `routingVocabulary` exemption that path segments get — and `redactUrls` then does a substring replace of each. Ordinary query values shipped by real plugins (`bridge-matrix` sends `timeout=30000`; `bridge-zulip` sends `dont_block=false`, `apply_markdown=false`, `include_anchor=true`, `anchor=newest`, `num_before=<n>`) are struck out of the untrusted body everywhere they appear, including inside longer words. This is the exact mirror of the defect the package already fixed for path segments ('keeps a method name in the body it explains'), and the existing table can never see it: every query-location row uses a 25+ character high-entropy token.
failure: url `https://api.example/v1/messages?ok=no&anchor=newest&num_before=10`, 400 body `Cannot send to stream; you have 100 messages and no permission (code 10)` → thrown message `Zulip GET → 400: Can<redacted>t send to stream; you have <redacted>0 messages and <redacted> permission (code <redacted>)`. Matrix: url `.../sync?filter=abc&since=s12345&timeout=30000`, body `{"error":"waited 30000 ms for room 30000abcd"}` → `waited <redacted> ms for room <redacted><redacted>d`. Both reproduced against the shipped module.
remediation: Apply the same `carriesSecret` predicate to query values as to path segments (length > ROUTE_WORD_CHARS and not routing vocabulary), so `access_token=<long opaque>` stays redacted while `false`, `true`, `newest`, `30000`, `10` survive; and make the replacement boundary-aware rather than raw substring, so a short value cannot chop a longer word in half.
testUpgrade: Widen the existing 'keeps %s in the body it explains' table into a component × value-shape cross-product: for each URL component (path segment, query value, userinfo) × each of [ordinary word, boolean literal, small integer, long opaque token], assert the ordinary/boolean/integer cells survive verbatim in the body and only the opaque cell is redacted. Generating the ordinary values from the query strings the shipped plugins actually build (grep `?…=` in packages/bridge-*/src) keeps the row set honest as backends change.

summary: `retryAfterFromHeader` tries the whole comma-joined header as one candidate and takes the max, but the HTTP-date branch defers to bare `Date.parse` — the very laxity the delay-seconds branch pins a regex against (`0x1F4`, `1e3`). V8 parses a joined multi-value header whose first field-value is a 4-digit number as a YEAR, producing a candidate that dominates the max by 12 orders of magnitude.
failure: `Retry-After: 3600` appended twice as `3600` and `5` (gateway + origin) → `Headers.get` yields `"3600, 5"`; `Date.parse("3600, 5")` = Jan 5 of year 3600 → `retryAfterFromHeader` returns 49_662_834_988_081 instead of 3_600_000. With `deadlineMs: 4_000_000` (which comfortably fits the hour the server actually asked for) the call ends immediately: `L → 429: upstream asked for 49662834988078ms, past this call's 4000000ms deadline (2ms elapsed). Raise deadlineMs to wait it out.` — advice no operator can act on.
remediation: Pin the HTTP-date spelling the way delay-seconds is pinned: accept only IMF-fixdate/RFC 850/asctime shapes before calling `Date.parse`, or only attempt the whole-raw candidate when the header does not split into two or more individually-parseable field-values.
testUpgrade: Add a table over multi-valued headers whose naive whole-string `Date.parse` succeeds — ['3600','5'], ['3600','12'], ['1900','1'] — plus the legitimate single HTTP-date (which contains its own comma), asserting in every row that the result equals the max of the field-values parsed INDIVIDUALLY. Generate the first element from a sweep of 1..4-digit second counts rather than hand-picking, so the next year-shaped figure is covered.

summary: In the credential-shape leak table, the LOCATIONS row 'a path segment' echoes the WHOLE pathname, which `carriesSecret` claims on the embedded `/12345/` whatever the token looks like — the file's own comment beside the next row says so. It is still crossed with all 15 SHAPES and 3 VECTORS, so 45 of the 180 cells exercise one identical code path and cannot independently fail; a reviewer reading the report cannot tell them from the 45 cells (the bare-segment row) that do grade the shape axis.
failure: Mutating METHOD_NAME_CHARS or ROUTE_WORD in src reddens the 'a path segment echoed on its own' cells; the 45 'a path segment' cells stay green for every shape, because the whole-pathname rule fires first. They cost a run and report as coverage of a shape axis they do not test.
remediation: Cross the SHAPES axis only with locations whose echoed fragment IS the bare component (segment-alone, userinfo, query value); keep the whole-path location as a single non-parameterized row asserting the pathname rule.
testUpgrade: Make the table generator assert its own discrimination: for each (location, shape) pair, record which redaction rule fired (whole-path / per-segment / userinfo / query) and require that within a location the shape axis produces more than one outcome, otherwise collapse it to one row. That check keeps every future cross-product from re-growing an inert axis.

summary: `http()` builds the header set from scratch (`Authorization` plus `Content-Type` when there is a body) and never sets a `User-Agent`. Discord's REST API documents that clients must supply a valid `User-Agent` (`DiscordBot ($url, $version)`) and states that requests without one may be blocked by Cloudflare.
failure: Reproduced the header set Node emits: `node -e` against a local server with the exact init `http()` builds gives `user-agent: node`. So every `POST /channels/<id>/messages`, `GET /channels/<id>/messages`, `GET /channels/<id>`, `GET /users/@me` and `GET /gateway/bot` reaches Discord identifying as `node`. The predicted production failure is a Cloudflare 403/1010 on the REST half — i.e. `post` and `fetchRecent` fail for every topic while nothing local reproduces it, because `fake-discord.ts` only inspects `Authorization` (test/fake-discord.ts:154). Marked PLAUSIBLE: the missing header and Node's default are confirmed by execution; Discord's rejection is inferred from its documented requirement, not reproduced against the live service.
remediation: Set `headers['User-Agent'] = 'DiscordBot (https://github.com/sharpTrick/parley, <package version>)'` in `http()`, sourced from the package version rather than hand-written, and add the same enforcement to the fake so it cannot be dropped.
testUpgrade: CLASS: 'a vendor-mandated request header that only the provider can miss' — the same class the `Authorization` rows in rest-contract.test.ts:539 already guard for credentials. Widen that table from `[Authorization variants]` to `[required header] x [every REST path the plugin calls: /users/@me, /gateway/bot, /channels/:id, /channels/:id/messages GET, /channels/:id/messages POST]`, have `fake-discord.ts` answer 403 when `user-agent` is absent or does not match `/^DiscordBot \(.+, .+\)$/`, and assert the version segment equals the package version so a stale literal loses a case.

summary: A short/partial `appendFileSync` leaves a fragment with no trailing newline and the store keeps writing at that offset, so the NEXT record is glued onto it and both are dropped at the next load — after `append` returned it as durable and `post` resolved with its backendMsgId.
failure: Reproduced with a synthetic fragment (the shape an ENOSPC/EIO short write leaves): store with record A; a partial line `{"chat_id":"-1","message_id":99,"se` on disk with no newline; `store.append(B)` returns a StoredRecord (so `post` resolves with `-1:2`); the file then reads `…{A}\n{"…"se{"…"content":"B"…}\n`; a fresh `new ObservedStore(path)` yields entries ['A'] and `has(keyOf(B)) === false`. B is unrecoverable — own posts never come back via getUpdates. The torn-tail repair only runs in the constructor, so a fragment created mid-run is never repaired by the process that made it.
remediation: Treat a throwing `appendFileSync` as leaving the file possibly torn: catch it in `append`, set a `torn` flag (and re-throw), and have the next successful append prefix its line with a newline (or re-open and truncate to a tracked good byte offset). Cheapest correct version: track the byte length written and `ftruncateSync` back to it on failure.
testUpgrade: Table over write-failure modes x ingest paths: {throws before any bytes, throws after a partial line, throws after a complete line} x {inbound update, own post}, asserting the invariant 'append returning a record implies that record is present after a cold reload, and append throwing implies the caller was told'. Drive the partial case by stubbing the store's write to emit half a line and throw. The existing 'store visibility and delivery' cells only inject a whole-call throw, which never leaves bytes on disk.
